items.title: "We are here to give you something to believe in": the former Disco Elysium devs of Summer Eternal reveal new RPG Red Rooster, a game of fire, water and alternate selves
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: Earlier this month, the former Disco Elysium developers of worker co-operative studio Summer Eternal sent me a 500-page anthology describing their new game Red
items.text:
Earlier this month, the former Disco Elysium developers of worker co-operative studio Summer Eternal sent me a 500-page anthology describing their new game Red Rooster. It's a 3D, real-time, third-person RPG you could broadly style as a spiritual Disco successor, working in the tradition of Planescape: Torment and Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines, but which also owes much inspiration to Baldur's Gate 3 and Dark Messiah of Might and Magic. It takes place in a magic realist, "our-world-adjacent", mightily flammable and divided river city called Arta-Tantor, created with Unreal Engine and housing a "physics-powered sandbox of objects you can individually move, manipulate – and burn."

Here, you will live out the story of Redrick Roost, a convict serving a life sentence after accidentally rendering thousands of people catatonic by means of an "auto-meditation" headset. Much like Disco's Harry, Redrick has a whole world of characters in his head – a hallucinatory vacuum shop or "chicken coop" full of alternate selves or "roosters", who vie for dominance as the game goes on, affecting your dialogue options and abilities. Redrick's broad goal, having been recruited by government spooks, is to identify the arsonist working at a fire station run by his own hero brother. You've got a week to pull this off before your parole hearing. Your colleagues include Dr Astrid Albers, a mathematician with an opiate problem who wakes up one day to find that mathematics has Gone Wrong.

Much like that last paragraph, the Summer Eternal book is a dense, knotty, wild-eyed thing. It's divided into two parts. The first is an account of Summer Eternal's formation that aims to situate the new studio within (and often, against) today's videogame industry and culture. There are essays on aesthetics, generative AI and the difficulty of pursuing anti-capitalist game development while being obliged to compromise a little for the sake of funding. There are open-ended interviews with several well-known game developers, including former BioWare devs Mark Darrah and David Gaider, together with sci-fi novelist Ted Chiang, Marxist economist Richard Wolff, and union organisers at United Videogame Workers-CWA. Also, a chat with those scruffy apparatchiks at indie journalist outfit Aftermath... and an acknowledgements page in which Summer Eternal thank myself and Mark Warren for our previous online coverage of the studio's founding. Look, we hacks have got to get some limelight now and then.

The book is further evidence that Summer Eternal are the most Marxist of the post-Disco studios. Put it this way: there is a double-page spread in which the eponymous red rooster is pictured striking down the vulture of venture capitalism, while studio founder and former ZA/UM narrative designer/principal writer Dora Klindžić decries "bourgeois virgins who administrate their battles from office desks".

At the risk of being branded a bourgeois virgin, I do think that Marxist writers can always benefit from some tactical self-deprecation – Disco Elysium was very good at seeing the funny side, and still had teeth as a political document. Still, this is a manifesto for a studio, not a piece of fiction, and I genuinely got a bit tearful about Klindžić's visions for a studio run for the benefit of workers and artists, in a universe that is being strangled by finance and cannibalised by LLMs. "We are preparing a conflagration, an end to mourning, an end to the poison fog of demoralization and the apathy tears of the mentally imprisoned," she writes. "With charred fingers, we are here to give you something to hope for. We are here to give you something to believe in."

More specifically, they are here to give us an RPG. The second half of the book is a massive pitch document and lore bible for Red Rooster, a game that is in the "early pre-production phase", with 3-4 years to go before release... providing Summer Eternal can pull together the funding. Obviously, the funding situation is a concern: I'd like to write more about the studio's structure, which divides shares between creatives and investors with a small portion set aside for fans. In the meantime, I'll say that Red Rooster sounds fascinating.

The section on Red Rooster opens with a lengthy fictional university essay about the history of Arta-Tantor, which is sort of three cities or "member-territories" nested close together - the result of centuries of war, rivalry and overseas exploitation with a broad theme of fire vs water. The city's factions include groups of heavily armed game wardens and couriers, together with a long-suffering fire service that originally consisted of slaves, and is now a mix of professionals, amateurs, and prisoners doing community service. Another, redacted in-world memorandum hints at a psionic organisation of some kind.

And then there's the cast. The book tells you a lot about Redrick and Astrid, including some details I'd rather you discover for yourself. Redrick's history is complicated, to say the least. His parents died in a house fire. At the age of 12, he was seduced by a school science teacher, who was later imprisoned not for statutory rape but commandeering a postal vehicle. As an adult, he fell in with the inventor of the aforesaid "auto-meditation" device, who capitalised on the infamy created by his "affair" for marketing purposes.

When the Baku headset malfunctioned, inducing "mass mental fracturing", it also gave rise to the Coop, Redrick's eerie inner sanctum, which is modelled after the vacuum shop he once worked in. Here, you'll spend XP to modify your build, while interacting with various Rooster-selves, who may form factions as they seek to dominate one another and shape Redrick's overall persona. Possible Roosters include a "Rooster-Raconteur" who can't stop debating people, a pathological gambler, and an "Overkompensaaator" who wears sunglasses indoors. More Roosters will appear as the game goes on, and you'll get to decide whether to admit, strengthen, and repress them to alter Redrick's stats and dialogue options, similar to the Copotypes in Disco Elysium. "Repression" is an actual dice-driven encounter, with several potential outcomes besides victory and failure. It's also possible for repressed or rejected Roosters to push through and hijack the Coop, if you continue to behave in a way that leans into their archetype.

Redrick's initial companion character Astrid, a maths prodigy working at a local research institute, isn't quite as messy, but she isn't exactly Miles Tails Prower either. She teams up with him after being caught overdosing on opiates and forced into a state-supervised rehabilitation program. Her job is to keep an eye on Redrick while he searches for the aforesaid arsonist. In the book, Astrid is defined by her claustrophobic relationship with her overbearing novelist father, her tendency to lie, and her realisation, one day, that the laws of mathematics have somehow altered, right down to the bones of the prime number system – an event that might have something to do with an on-going heatwave.

There is much to say about Astrid, but all I'll add for the moment is that her visual inspirations include Patti Smith and Gollum. She has stage presence for lightyears, while Redrick is characterised as earnest and apologetic and not-quite-there. Redrick can bolster his look using a rhizomatic clothing system where you set up fashion synergies on a grid, rather than the usual equipment screen in which clothing is categorised by body part.

If these characters are absolutely the kind of people you'd expect to meet in Disco Elysium, Red Rooster cleaves from that inspiration with its unhealthy interest in physics. There's a chapter in the book where game director Argo Tuulik frames the game's manipulable object world as a key point of differentiation: "this visceral connection, developed through a myriad of small interactions that form the all-encompassing connective tissue, is the holy grail. The missing physical counterpart to the ultra-reactive psychological role-play. The logical next step in the RPG genre. It is the most important pillar of Red Rooster."

The game will, amongst other things, allow you to lob and break objects with different weight, fragility and elasticity, from chairs to bike tyres. A "simplified but realistic real-time fire simulation" plays out Redrick's torturous relationship with fire, spreading between surfaces according to material properties: by the sounds of things, acts of arson are how you'll pursue particular subplots and revelations, though not everything in the world can burn.

The world is also subject to change and entropy, independent of your activities: lightbulbs will burn out, falling leaves will cover staircases, trash bags will be emptied, local sculptors will slowly turn hunks of stone into statues. These unfolding phenomena sit within a web of 'terrain factors' imposed by Arta-Trantor's weird tripartite political culture, with a "topologically complex map where international borders criss-cross the streets, bisect buildings and bedroms, and create enclaves and counter-enclaves within the same neighbourhoods".

The devs say you'll move across a multitude of "soft borders" as you explore, which creates bizarre possibilities and constraints. You might cross a street to move into a different jurisdiction and thereby throw off a cop. You might cross a bar when the clock strikes 10pm to carry on drinking in a territory where it's legal to sell booze until 2am. Or you might have to make use of a window to get around a revised border policy, rather than opening the front door.

I'll end by stressing that Summer Eternal is still far more pitch for a game than a game. Much of the above may change, and the developers make no secret of the fact that they're still raising funds. But they've certainly sketched out some wonderful, macabre territory. I'm especially keen on all the hypnotic rhetoric around fire, as somebody who's written a bit here and there about procedural fire systems in videogames. I'll likely be diving back into the book for more stories. In the meantime, you can order a copy yourself via the official website.

You might cross a street to move into a different jurisdiction and thereby throw off a cop. You might cross a bar when the clock strikes 10pm to carry on drinking in a territory where it's legal to sell booze until 2am. Or you might have to make use of a window to get around a revised border policy, rather than opening the front door.

I'll end by stressing that Summer Eternal is still far more pitch for a game than a game. Much of the above may change, and the developers make no secret of the fact that they're still raising funds. But they've certainly sketched out some wonderful, macabre territory. I'm especially keen on all the hypnotic rhetoric around fire, as somebody who's written a bit here and there about procedural fire systems in videogames. I'll likely be diving back into the book for more stories. In the meantime, you can order a copy yourself via the official website.

items.text:
Steam Officially Makes 2 Hit Games 100% Free Until October 19

Published Oct 16, 2026, 5:24 AM EDT

Sharmila is an engineer-turned-gaming hardware journalist and freelance contributor at ScreenRant who has been covering the gaming and tech industry since 2021. While she first built her expertise writing about video games, she has since pivoted towards gaming hardware, with a focus on PC components, peripherals, handhelds, and performance-driven tech. When she’s not testing gear or writing about the latest hardware trends, she can usually be found diving into competitive shooters or keeping up with the evolving esports scene.

Steam has a busy couple of days lined up for PC gamers, with two very different and popular games available to play for free until October 19. Whether you want to try surviving on a deserted island or jump into large-scale military battles, you’re pretty much sorted for the weekend.

With Steam, PC gamers frequently get chances to try titles without spending money upfront. Its limited-time free-play promotions are particularly useful for those who want to test a game’s mechanics, see how it performs on their system, or decide whether it’s worth buying before committing to the full price.

Test Your Survival Skills In Stranded Deep, Free For Limited Time

Stranded Deep drops you in the middle of the Pacific Ocean after a mysterious plane crash and has you tackle the worst from there. With no immediate way to call for help, players must find supplies, craft tools, gather food, and build shelter while trying to stay alive.

The challenges extend beyond finding somewhere to sleep. Players must manage hunger, thirst, and exposure while exploring islands and searching underwater locations for useful resources. Dangerous wildlife and the possibility of running out of essential supplies make every expedition a potential risk. You can play Stranded Deep alone or with a friend, so you can always choose to share your challenges with someone if flying solo is too much.

According to the official Steam store page, Stranded Deep is free to play until October 19 at 10 a.m. PT. It’s also discounted during the promotion, so you have an opportunity to purchase it at a lower price (60% off, at $7.99) if you enjoy their time during the free trial. The timing also coincides with renewed attention around the franchise, with a developer update published on October 15 discussing Stranded Deep 2 and introducing details about its desert environment and wildlife. Players interested in the sequel can add it to their Steam wishlist.

Battlefield 6 Is Also Free To Play on Steam Until October 19

Players who would rather trade survival crafting for firefights can check out Battlefield 6. Released back in 2025, the military shooter features battles involving infantry, tanks, fighter jets, and a range of modern weapons.

Unlike Stranded Deep, Battlefield 6 focuses on fast-paced combat across large and unique battlefields. Its multiplayer experience offers several ways to fight in different modes, while Battlefield Portal gives players additional ways to engage with the game’s maps and gameplay.

The Battlefield 6 free trial runs from October 15 through October 19. According to the publisher’s official access guide, players can access the full game during the trial, including all its available game modes, events, and Battlefield Portal. Needless to say, this is a great offer for anyone who has Battlefield 6 wishlisted for a long time but hasn’t wanted to pay for it without trying it first. The game is also on discount on Steam during the promotion. Players who decide to buy it after the trial can get it at a whopping 60% off, taking the price down to $27.99.

To download Stranded Deep and Battlefield 6 during the free event, open the official Steam store page for either, sign in to your Steam account, and select the option to play for free to install it. Both promotions (free play period) end on October 19, so you shouldn’t wait until the last minute to begin downloading—or they won’t get the time to play at all. Battlefield 6 also requires an EA account linked to Steam, along with a persistent internet connection.

Remember that these are free-play offers on Steam, not free-to-keep deals. Access to the full versions ends when the promotions expire unless you purchase them. Battlefield REDSEC, however, remains a separate free-to-play experience.

items.text:
Digger is not exactly bringing audiences to the cinema, but it’s certainly inciting conversation amongst those who’ve seen it. Despite its poor performance at the box office, the ranks of Digger fans continue to grow and now include the creator of Metal Gear. Hideo Kojima praised the film for how it tackles its themes and ideas and, in a conversation with its director, Alejandro González Iñárritu, even compared the film’s narrative to his own game Metal Gear Solid 2.

After calling Digger “a film that all of us living in today’s world should see” on his social media accounts, Kojima expanded on why he felt that way in an interview with Iñárritu for Gizmodo Japan. The film, which dives deep into climate catastrophe and misinformation in the form of both comedy and intense drama, drew comparisons to movies like Stanley Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove and Charlie Chaplin’s The Great Dictator in how it forces audiences to examine the current state of the world by abstracting it into absurdist satire.

“It’s not a story where meteorites fall from the sky or aliens attack, instead capturing things that are actually happening in reality,” Kojima says of the film. “It’s also a very terrifying movie, but it feels like that’s precisely why they managed to make it a comedy. It feels like a film whose structure combines both cinema and theater, and in the end becomes a play presented not as something set in the future but as a part of our history. That structure is so well done it actually surprised me.”

He notes that these aspects in particular remind him of the social commentary present in Metal Gear Solid 2. “Back then we didn’t have social media, but the story I made was one where social media took on a life of its own,” Kojima explained to Iñárritu. “That’s a bit like what’s happening in Digger too, isn’t it? On social media sites misinformation spreads quickly, and there’s a fear over how this has an impact on politics and our daily lives. Here, too, I found Digger to be very similar structurally. As if stepping into the movie’s world, I felt a sense of fear, like we were being driven by forces beyond our control. Right now, aside from climate change, the thing that scares us all most is the possibility we’re lost in a digital world where we can’t tell what’s true.”

Iñárritu agrees with Kojima’s line of thinking, noting he has a fear that we’re losing touch with a shared reality that can connect us as we live instead inside “fragmented truths within our smartphones”. “Even the conversations taking place about the film are fueled not by the movie itself but the stories that surround it,” he continues. “Even people who haven’t seen it yet have strong opinions on it. Our current world is one of having firm convictions on things we haven’t even experienced.”

Here, too, Kojima was reminded of his own experiences. “I made a game called Death Stranding where you go around making deliveries, but people who hadn’t even played it were saying it was ‘just a walking simulator’ as though they’d actually played it!” he says. “That perception still persists now, and the way it can scares me the most. On top of that, of course, we have AI being integrated into social media, and you only end up seeing things you like. You’re seeing only the opinions and things you like, so differing opinions and ideas never reach you.

“As AI becomes more prominent, becoming almost like a concierge, we might end up in a situation where we only eat the foods we like or only meet people who share our views. It’s like we’re being manipulated by someone, like the people in Digger. We don’t know who or what’s behind it. That’s what’s so terrifying, and it’s why I want you to see this movie.”

Kojima’s love of film is no secret, and as he experiments with moving into film himself through his work with A24, he has bridged a gap between the games and cinema and considered where they are similar and where they diverge. Much like Backrooms whose director he also connected with, Digger is a film whose creator Kojima has found a kindred spirit in, sharing concerns for the future in the process. Maybe he should take up work as a full-time film critic when he finishes work on OD and Physint.

items.title: Activision’s Head Marketer Says Modern Warfare 4 Faces A ‘Call Of Duty Tax’
items.author: Ethan Gach
items.summary: A new Call of Duty has come out every fall for over 20 years. While still an annual best-seller, the franchise’s cultural cachet has shifted over the last 10
items.text:
A new Call of Duty has come out every fall for over 20 years. While still an annual best-seller, the franchise’s cultural cachet has shifted over the last 10 years. With the rise of live-service games, Call of Duty has become its own massive silo within the wider world of online multiplayer. Where new Call of Duty releases were once treated as tech-defining showcases, they now feel more like the arrival of a new Madden or NBA 2K. Activision chief marketing officer Tyler Bahl calls this the Call of Duty tax.

“We get the coverage,” he said in a new interview with The Game Business. “But we call it the Call of Duty tax, when we’re thinking about the reviews or the reception. There’s obviously a lot of fandom around indie games and excitement around new games popping up every day on Steam. And Call of Duty’s been here for a very long time, and with that people sometimes forget that there’s so much work that goes into making these games. There’s 4,500 employees here that are trying to make the best possible experience.”

Like each new annualized sports franchise release, which often reviews poorly but sells spectacularly, Call of Duty games rarely get scored well by critics these days. Once consistently in the high 70s and low 80s on Metacritic, the shooter series is now just as likely to appear in the mid-60s, a yellow-coded range that shouts “bad game” in a landscape saturated with amazing games. 2024’s Call of Duty: Black Ops 6 bucked this trend with an 83. Last year’s sequel, Black Ops 7, was a 65. And 2023’s Modern Warfare 3, the game this year’s entry is a sequel to, sank to a franchise-low Metacritic score of 56 on PS5.

“We have 100 million free-to-play players, we’ve sold 500 million units, it’s one of the biggest franchises of all time, and we have a billion downloads on mobile,” Bahl said. “And so that huge audience, I think, sometimes, gets overlooked or just becomes status quo. There’s craft that goes into these games, and the dedication from the teams was something that we wanted to show this year with the marketing.”

But the Call of Duty tax isn’t just a vibes issue. Regardless of bored critics or the changing media landscape around live-service game releases, Call of Duty‘s struggles are showing up in the player numbers as well. The Game Business points to data estimates from Ampere Analysis that show a massive dip in monthly active users for Call of Duty since the launch of Black Ops 7. Over the summer, it sank to an estimated 20 million players, half of where it had been. The only thing that saved it was the surprise release of ports for Black Ops 1 and 2, a dose of nostalgia and a reminder of the good old days when Call of Duty was one of the top dogs, both commercially and culturally.

“It was not something that our community was looking for,” Bahl said on the topic of Black Ops 7. “They wanted something fresh, and even though there were different time settings, and ways to play the game with new features, that tonal shift is something that they were looking for. So, we’ve already stated that a future title is going to be a new sub-franchise and we’ve already laid the groundwork. But we’re really excited about Modern Warfare 4, and that addresses some of that feedback.”

The new Modern Warfare campaign goes live for players who purchase the early access edition starting October 16.

Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Remake Officially Unveils Dark Link Redesign

Published Oct 16, 2026, 6:01 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is painfully close to launch. November 5, 2026, is mere weeks away and fans of the greatest adventure game of all time are itching for some sneaky peaks before the game's release. Will it be faithful to the original with just a visual overhaul, or can we expect new content? Well, only time will tell as Nintendo are keeping fairly tight-lipped. What we have just learned, though, is how awesome Shadow Link looks in the remake. Let's get into it!

A quick GIF reveal over on X, shows a couple of frames of the legendary foe in action. Anyone old enough to remember the late nighties will recall coming up against this absolute badass. Sure, some say the screeching ReDead are terrifying or the gruesome Dead Hand sticks in your mind after playing. But really, the biggest sweaty palms moment in the whole game is when you go toe to toe against Shadow Link, also known as Dark Link to some.

The brief clip is enough to bring back that sense of dread. From the dark foggy area, to the reflections in the water, this first encounter with Dark Link is truly terrifying. And the clip captures his deadliness in one swift movement. While targeting Dark Link, our plucky hero lunges forward with his sword only for Dark Link to backflip and land expertly on the side of the blade. A big screw you to anyone feeling like they were good at combat. It takes the Dark Souls 'git gud' motto and runs with it. Dark Link is an impressive foe not to be messed with.

The brief animation comes thanks to Genki_JPN over on X and does a lot to showcase, even in the briefest of moments, how impressive this opponent is. items.text:
Apple TV's New Crown Jewel Officially Continues Streaming Domination

Image: Robert Clark/Apple TV

Published Oct 16, 2026, 5:30 AM EDT

Denis is a news writer for Collider with close to five years of experience in the industry. He has analyzed shows across different genres, formats and styles. His favorite types of articles to write are exciting news updates and episodic deep-dives. He might say he doesn't have a favorite show, but he has watched The Wire, Shameless, The Big Bang Theory, and The Blacklist more than once. Denis is increasingly becoming focused on the global streaming arena and how media connects with audiences in various markets. Find him on X tweeting about something random that occurred to him about a TV show or the industry in general.

For the past half-decade plus, Apple TV has built its reputation as a premium entertainment destination. It has slowly risen from a fledgling streamer initially thought of as a side project for Apple to a major television and movie player. The journey has been slow but steady as the service has claimed its place in the sci-fi and thriller space. It has also drawn major awards attention and become a serious threat to the likes of Netflix and HBO.

Many Apple TV shows are considered successes thanks to engaging stories and top-tier production quality, even when the service has never revealed raw viewership numbers. The streamer also offers a variety of stories, championing both book-to-series adaptations and original ideas. Its first major hit arrived in 2020 when Ted Lasso premiered to critical and audience acclaim. But before that, shows such as The Morning Show also attracted attention with their timely stories and strong casts. This year, however, Apple TV landed its new smash hit, which has become a streaming sensation and broken records for Emmy wins and nominations.

This show was a slight departure from what Apple TV is known for, but it wasn't any less good. It blended genres to deliver a fresh, entertaining story that critics immediately recognized, earning a near-perfect 98% on Rotten Tomatoes. Viewers were not far behind, giving the dramedy a 92%. It's been months since the series Widow's Bay completed its first season, but that hasn't stopped it on streaming. Streaming rankings from FlixPatrol show the horror comedy is still one of Apple TV's most-streamed shows, ranking fifth at the time of writing. This is no minor feat for a new show with only eight episodes, as most new shows fall off a month after the season finale.

Collider Exclusive · 8 Questions · 2 Minutes
What Is Your Biggest Horror Nightmare?
Elm Street · Chucky · Scream · The Conjuring

Four horror franchises. Four completely different ways of scaring you. One waits until you fall asleep. One makes sure nobody believes you. One is already in your group of friends. And one is in the house with your family. Answer eight quick questions about how you actually watch horror, and find out which nightmare was built for you.

😴Elm Street(Freddy Krueger)

🧸Chucky(Child's Play)

📞Scream(Ghostface)

🕯️The Conjuring(The Warren Files)

FIND YOUR NIGHTMARE →

01

Which horror scene makes you cover your eyes?
Four classic images. One of them is worse than the others for you.

ASomebody falling asleep when they really should not.
BA toy that has moved, and nobody touched it.
CA phone ringing in an empty house.
DA child talking to somebody who is not there.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

You are home alone and you hear a noise. First thought?
Everybody has one. It arrives before you have decided anything.

AI am exhausted and my mind is playing tricks on me.
BSomething in this room is not where I left it.
CSomebody is in here with me.
DThis house has never felt entirely right.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

Which horror movie rule would you break first?
Everybody thinks they would survive. Almost nobody actually does.

ANever fall asleep.
BNever leave it out of your sight.
CNever answer the phone.
DNever go down to the basement.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

Something genuinely frightening happens. What do you do?
Not in a film. In your actual living room, tonight.

AConvince myself I imagined the whole thing.
BTell someone, and brace for them not believing me.
CWork out which person I know could be behind it.
DGet everybody in the house into one room.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How do you actually watch a horror film?
Be honest about this one. Nobody is checking.

AFine during. Wide awake at two in the morning.
BShouting at the screen that nobody is listening.
CCalling the twist out loud before it lands.
DThrough my fingers, holding on to something.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Somebody offers you serious money. Which do you still refuse?
The amount does not matter. There is one on this list you are not doing.

AFall asleep in a room I have never been in before.
BKeep an old doll on the shelf facing my bed.
CAnswer every unknown number that calls after midnight.
DSpend one night alone in a house with a history.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Which feeling stays with you a week after the film?
Good horror does not stop when the credits do.

ANot wanting to turn the bedroom light off.
BNot trusting one particular object in my house.
CLooking twice at people I have known for years.
DFeeling like something came home with me.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

Something wakes you at 3am. What is the worst possibility?
Eight questions in, this is the one that decides your nightmare.

AThat I am still asleep, and it knows it.
BThat the thing nobody believed me about is here.
CThat somebody with a key is downstairs.
DThat something is in the doorway, watching us sleep.

REVEAL MY NIGHTMARE →

The Lights Just Went Out
Your Nightmare Is…

Four franchises, four completely different ways of getting underneath
your skin. This is the one built out of your particular fear, why it works so well on you, and what
it would leave behind.

A Nightmare on Elm Street · Since 1984

Elm Street

Your nightmare does not wait outside the door. It waits for you
to close your eyes, which you are going to have to do eventually, because nobody has ever
won that particular argument.

Freddy is horror's cruellest idea: a threat that lives in the one place you cannot
guard, cannot lock, and cannot avoid forever.

You are the one who is fine during the film and wide awake at two in the morning. Your
own head is where this does its damage.

These films understood exhaustion as a horror engine. The kids on Elm Street do not lose
because they are weak. They lose because they are tired.

You can lock every door in the house. You still have to sleep.

Child's Play · Chucky · Since 1988

Chucky

Your nightmare is not really the doll. It is the face of the
person you tell, and the way they decide, very kindly, that you have imagined all of it.

Chucky works precisely because he is absurd. That is the trap: the more accurately you
describe him, the less anybody is going to believe you.

You are the one shouting at the screen because the characters are not listening. You
know that feeling from real life too.

The franchise is at its best when the adults in the room are the real obstacle, and you
have met those adults.

By the time somebody finally believes you, you will have handled most of it on your own.

Scream · Ghostface · Since 1996

Scream

Your nightmare has your number, knows your name, and has almost
certainly been inside your house before. The worst part is that you already know them.

Scream is the only one of these where the killer takes the mask off and turns out to be
somebody who was at the party.

You are the person who calls the twist out loud before it lands. You watch people the
same way you watch films.

The franchise made the rules of horror part of the plot, which means the survivors are
the ones paying attention. You would be paying attention.

Everybody is a suspect, including the person who just offered to walk you home.

The Conjuring · The Warren Files · Since 2013

The Conjuring

Your nightmare is not really about you. It is about the people
asleep down the hall, and the feeling that whatever is here is not interested in leaving.

The Conjuring films are domestic horror. The house, the family, the perfectly ordinary
room that quietly stops feeling ordinary.

Your instinct is to get everybody into one room. Your fear is protective rather than
personal, which is rarer than it sounds.

This is the one franchise where belief is the weapon. The people who come through it are
the ones who are not alone and refuse to be.

Whatever is here did not come for you. It came for the household, and you are the one
standing in the hallway.

Published Oct 16, 2026, 5:22 AM EDT

In over three years at Collider, senior author Jake has now penned over 3000 articles covering a wide range of TV and film for the resources, lists, utilities, news, and interview teams. Alongside interviewing stars such as Selin Hizli, Rose Ayling-Ellis, Harlan Coben, and Chelsea Peretti, Jake was lucky enough to visit the set of Aardman and Netflix's Wallace and Gromit: A Vengeance Most Fowl in 2024, getting the chance to chat with four-time Academy Award winner Nick Park and Merlin Crossingham. Jake has also worked for other publications, including Agents of Fandom. You can also hear Jake every week as the resident film and TV journalist on Track Radio.

Rob Savage's Other Mommy, a brand-new horror starring Academy Award winner Jessica Chastain, might've topped the box office last weekend, but it faces fresh competition this weekend. Its biggest rival is Street Fighter, Kitao Sakurai's star-studded adaptation of the popular video game franchise featuring many Hollywood faces preparing for the World Warrior Tournament. There is also competition from the latest adaptation of Jane Austen’s Sense and Sensibility and the survival thriller Whalefall, but Other Mommy will hope to prove popular in a second weekend. As the box office fight goes on, you might prefer to get your entertainment from the small screen. With that in mind, here's a look at three movies you should watch this weekend on Netflix.

Disclaimer: These titles are available on US Netflix.

1
'Cocaine Bear' (2023)

Rotten Tomatoes: 65% | IMDb: 5.9/10

The appeal of a streamer like Netflix is its ever-revolving door of new arrivals. Earlier this week, one of the most bonkers movies of the decade so far made its move to Netflix and should be right at the top of your watchlist. The comedy thriller Cocaine Bear, directed by Elizabeth Banks, follows a group of cops, criminals, tourists, and teens as they face the threat of a black bear's drug-fueled rampage.

Remarkably based on a true story from 1985, Cocaine Bear is a stranger-than-fiction tale that will keep you glued to the edge of your seat. What is even more bonkers is the film's cast, which is not only packed with talent that includes Keri Russell, Alden Ehrenreich, O’Shea Jackson Jr., Brooklynn Prince, and Margo Martindale but also marks one of the final performances in the great career of the late Ray Liotta.

Collider Exclusive · Action Hero Quiz
Which Action Hero Would Be
Your Perfect Partner?
Rambo · James Bond · Indiana Jones · John McClane · Ethan Hunt

Five legends. Five completely different ways of getting out alive — with style, with muscle, with charm, with luck, or with a plan so intricate it probably shouldn't work. Ten questions will reveal which action hero was built to have your back.

🎖️Rambo

🍸James Bond

🏺Indiana Jones

🔧John McClane

🎭Ethan Hunt

FIND YOUR PARTNER →

01

You're dropped into a dangerous situation with no warning. What do you need most from a partner?
The first few seconds tell you everything about who belongs beside you.

ASomeone who already has three contingency plans running and is calmly working through all of them.
BSomeone who reads the terrain instinctively and knows exactly how to use it against the enemy.
CSomeone who keeps their nerve and their sense of humour when everything is falling apart.
DSomeone who knows the history of wherever we are and what we're walking into.
ESomeone with the right contact, the right cover identity, and the right exit already arranged.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

You have to get somewhere dangerous, fast. How do you travel?
How you get there is half the mission.

AOn foot through terrain no one else would attempt — I move where vehicles can't follow.
BOn a motorcycle, a cargo plane, or anything else that gets me there before I think too hard about it.
CIn something that belongs to someone else — borrowed, stolen, or improvised under fire.
DFirst class, with a cover identity and a gadget that does something I won't explain until it's needed.
EBy whatever means are available — I've driven, flown, and once arrived by camel. The destination matters, not the method.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

You're pinned down and outnumbered. What does your ideal partner do?
This is when you find out what someone is really made of.

ADisappears into the environment, flanks them silently, and ends it before I've reloaded.
BCracks a one-liner, grabs a fire extinguisher or a chair, and improvises something that somehow works.
CProduces a gadget specifically designed for this exact scenario and uses it with infuriating precision.
DPulls out a whip, a pistol, and an archaeological insight that somehow gets us out alive.
ENeutralises the threat with maximum efficiency and minimum words — they were already three moves ahead.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

The mission is paused. You have one evening to decompress. What does your partner suggest?
Who someone is when the pressure drops is who they actually are.

AA bar with terrible lighting, cold beer, and absolutely no questions about feelings.
BThe finest restaurant in the city, a bottle of something expensive, and a conversation that is equal parts brilliant and exhausting.
CA local dig site, a museum after hours, or a long story about why that particular artefact matters to human civilisation.
DPizza. Bad TV. Falling asleep halfway through a movie neither of you were watching anyway.
EA debrief that turns into three hours of contingency planning that somehow becomes the most fun you've had all week.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How do you prefer your partner to communicate mid-mission?
Good communication is the difference between partners and a liability.

APrecise and minimal — tell me what I need to know and nothing else. Every word has a cost.
BDeadpan and dry — keeping it light keeps me sharp, even when everything is on fire.
CEnthusiastic and slightly chaotic — but always with useful information buried somewhere in the noise.
DCalm and controlled through an earpiece, with a plan that covers every variable I haven't thought of yet.
EBarely at all — silence is a language and they speak it fluently.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Your enemy is powerful, well-resourced, and has the upper hand. How should your partner approach them?
The approach to the enemy defines the partnership.

AInfiltrate their inner circle, learn everything, and dismantle them from inside out before they know we're there.
BStudy the historical pattern — every villain of this type has a weakness written somewhere in the past.
CGet them talking. The more they monologue, the more time I have to figure out how to beat them.
DGo through them. Directly. With as much force as the terrain allows.
EFind the one thing they haven't accounted for — there's always one thing — and make sure we're holding it.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Things go badly wrong and you're captured. What do you trust your partner to do?
Who someone is when you need them most is the only thing that matters.

ACome in alone, quietly, and get me out before anyone knows they were there.
BHave already been working on the extraction since the moment I disappeared — the plan is already running.
CCome in loud, come in fast, and worry about the collateral damage later — I'd do the same for them.
DUse every resource, every contact, and bend every rule until I'm out — they don't leave people behind.
ECharm their way in somehow, bluff through the hard part, and still manage to look good doing it.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What does your ideal partner bring to the table that you couldn't replace?
A great partner fills the gap you didn't know you had.

ATechnology that shouldn't exist yet and the training to use it under any conditions.
BSurvival instinct so refined it borders on supernatural — and the scars to prove it's been tested.
CKnowledge of history, language, and culture that makes them invaluable in places where force is useless.
DThe ability to walk into any room in the world and immediately become the most trusted person in it.
EStubbornness that refuses to accept a situation is hopeless — and the improvisational skill to back it up.

NEXT QUESTION →

09

Every partnership has a cost. Which of these can you live with?
No one comes without baggage. The question is whether you can carry it together.

AA partner who never fully switches off — always watching exits, always calculating threats, even at dinner.
BA partner who gets the job done brilliantly but has the emotional availability of a locked filing cabinet.
CA partner who makes everything ten times more complicated than it needs to be — but who always comes through.
DA partner who gets personally attached to every relic, ruin, and artefact we encounter, which slows everything down.
EA partner who was not built for this and knows it — but shows up anyway, every time, without being asked.

NEXT QUESTION →

10

It's the final moment. Everything is on the line. What do you need from your partner right now?
The last question is the most honest one.

AOne line. Absolutely dry. Delivered like the world isn't ending. Then we move.
BNothing said at all — just a look that means we both already know what has to happen.
CA plan I don't fully understand that somehow accounts for everything, delivered in thirty seconds flat.
DA piece of historical context that reframes the entire situation and tells us exactly what to do next.
ESomeone who steps forward instead of back — because that's who they've always been.

REVEAL MY PARTNER →

Your Partner Has Been Assigned
Your Perfect Partner Is…

Your answers have pointed to one action hero above all others. This is the person built to have your back — for better or considerably, spectacularly worse.

Rambo

Your partner doesn't talk much, doesn't need to, and will have assessed every threat in your immediate environment before you've finished your first sentence. John Rambo is not a man of plans or politics — he is a force of nature shaped by survival, loyalty, and a capacity for endurance that goes beyond anything training can produce. He will not leave you behind. He has never left anyone behind who deserved to come home. What you get with Rambo is the most capable, most quietly ferocious partner imaginable — one who has been through things that would have broken anyone else, and who chose to keep going anyway. You'll never need to ask if he has your back. You'll just know.

James Bond

Your partner will arrive perfectly dressed, perfectly briefed, and with a cover story so convincing it'll take you a moment to remember what's actually true. James Bond is the most professionally dangerous person in any room he enters — and the most disarmingly charming, which is the point. He operates in a world of layers, where nothing is what it appears and every advantage is used without apology. You'll never be bored. You'll occasionally be furious. But when it matters — when the mission is genuinely on the line and the margin for error has collapsed to nothing — Bond is exactly the partner you want. He has survived things that have no business being survivable. He does it with style. That is not nothing.

Indiana Jones

Your partner will know the history, the language, the cultural context, and exactly why the thing everyone else is ignoring is actually the most important thing in the room. Indiana Jones is brilliant, reckless, and occasionally impossible — but he is also one of the most resourceful, most genuinely knowledgeable partners you could find yourself beside. He approaches every situation with a scholar's eye and a brawler's instinct, which is an unusual combination and a remarkably effective one. He hates snakes and gets personally attached to objects of historical significance, both of which will slow you down at least once. It doesn't matter. What Indy brings is irreplaceable — and the adventures you'll have together will be the kind people write books about. Assuming you survive them.

John McClane

Your partner was not supposed to be here. He does not have the right equipment, the right information, or anything approaching the right odds. He has a sarcastic remark and an absolute refusal to accept that the situation is as bad as it looks. John McClane is the greatest accidental hero in the history of action cinema — a man whose superpower is stubbornness, whose contingency plan is improvisation, and whose capacity to absorb punishment and keep moving would be alarming if it weren't so useful. He will complain the entire time. He will make it significantly more chaotic than it needed to be. And he will absolutely, unconditionally, without question come through when it counts. Yippee-ki-yay.

Ethan Hunt

Your partner has already run seventeen scenarios by the time you've finished reading the briefing, and the plan he's settled on involves at least two things that should be physically impossible. Ethan Hunt operates at the absolute edge of human capability — technically, physically, and intellectually — and he brings the same relentless precision to protecting his partners that he brings to dismantling organisations that shouldn't exist. He is not easy to know and he will never fully tell you everything. But he will carry the weight of the mission so completely, so absolutely, that your job is simply to trust him — and the remarkable thing is that trusting him always turns out to be the right call. The mission will be impossible. He will complete it anyway.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

2
'Heat' (1995)

Rotten Tomatoes: 84% | IMDb: 8.3/10

Another new arrival on Netflix this past week is much less divisive. In fact, it is considered the greatest crime thriller ever made by some. Writer/director Michael Mann's magnum opus, Heat, stars Robert De Niro and Al Pacino in the ultimate tale of cat-and-mouse as a group of criminals leaves behind a clue for the LAPD.

One of the most famous snubs in Academy Awards history, Heat might've gone unrecognized at the Oscars, but that hasn't stopped it from earning the sort of perfect legacy most other movies could only dream of. Almost three hours long but flying by at a frantic pace, Heat also stars the likes of Diane Venora, Natalie Portman, Amy Brenneman, and Val Kilmer. With a sequel finally confirmed, and Leonardo DiCaprio, Christian Bale, and Stephen Graham lined up to star, don't miss out on Heat now.

3
'Babes' (2024)

Rotten Tomatoes: 87% | IMDb: 6.3/10

This feature directorial debut by Pamela Adlon is written by and stars ​​Ilana Glazer as Eden, who, alongside lifelong friend Dawn (Michelle Buteau), faces the difficult battle of adulthood in modern New York City. However, their long-lasting friendship faces its biggest test when Eden decides to have a baby on her own after a one-night stand.

Survival of the Thickest star Buteau and Glazer have perfect chemistry in this heartfelt and intelligent comedy that will add a shine to your weekend. "Babes doesn’t squander its comedic potential nor miss serving omnipresent views on childbirth that address its tortures, sorrows, and not-so-dreamy realities," wrote Matthew Donato in Collider's official review.

Release Date

May 17, 2024

Runtime

109 Minutes

Director

Pamela Adlon

Writers

Ilana Glazer, Josh Rabinowitz

Your partner doesn't talk much, doesn't need to, and will have assessed every threat in your immediate environment before you've finished your first sentence. John Rambo is not a man of plans or politics — he is a force of nature shaped by survival, loyalty, and a capacity for endurance that goes beyond anything training can produce. He will not leave you behind. He has never left anyone behind who deserved to come home. What you get with Rambo is the most capable, most quietly ferocious partner imaginable — one who has been through things that would have broken anyone else, and who chose to keep going anyway. You'll never need to ask if he has your back. You'll just know.
James Bond
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/11/spectrum-on-demand-logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

Your partner will arrive perfectly dressed, perfectly briefed, and with a cover story so convincing it'll take you a moment to remember what's actually true. James Bond is the most professionally dangerous person in any room he enters — and the most disarmingly charming, which is the point. He operates in a world of layers, where nothing is what it appears and every advantage is used without apology. You'll never be bored. You'll occasionally be furious. But when it matters — when the mission is genuinely on the line and the margin for error has collapsed to nothing — Bond is exactly the partner you want. He has survived things that have no business being survivable. He does it with style. That is not nothing.
Indiana Jones

Your partner will know the history, the language, the cultural context, and exactly why the thing everyone else is ignoring is actually the most important thing in the room. Indiana Jones is brilliant, reckless, and occasionally impossible — but he is also one of the most resourceful, most genuinely knowledgeable partners you could find yourself beside. He approaches every situation with a scholar's eye and a brawler's instinct, which is an unusual combination and a remarkably effective one. He hates snakes and gets personally attached to objects of historical significance, both of which will slow you down at least once. It doesn't matter. What Indy brings is irreplaceable — and the adventures you'll have together will be the kind people write books about. Assuming you survive them.
John McClane

Your partner was not supposed to be here. He does not have the right equipment, the right information, or anything approaching the right odds. He has a sarcastic remark and an absolute refusal to accept that the situation is as bad as it looks. John McClane is the greatest accidental hero in the history of action cinema — a man whose superpower is stubbornness, whose contingency plan is improvisation, and whose capacity to absorb punishment and keep moving would be alarming if it weren't so useful. He will complain the entire time. He will make it significantly more chaotic than it needed to be. And he will absolutely, unconditionally, without question come through when it counts. Yippee-ki-yay.
Ethan Hunt
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/11/plex-logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

Your partner has already run seventeen scenarios by the time you've finished reading the briefing, and the plan he's settled on involves at least two things that should be physically impossible. Ethan Hunt operates at the absolute edge of human capability — technically, physically, and intellectually — and he brings the same relentless precision to protecting his partners that he brings to dismantling organisations that shouldn't exist. He is not easy to know and he will never fully tell you everything. But he will carry the weight of the mission so completely, so absolutely, that your job is simply to trust him — and the remarkable thing is that trusting him always turns out to be the right call. The mission will be impossible. He will complete it anyway.

items.text:
Medical dramas are typically among the most reliable genres that a network or streamer can tap into for sustained success. Most weeks, the Nielsen streaming charts feature Grey's Anatomy, arguably the most successful medical drama of all time. The opportunity is always there to produce a new hit that can take up the mantle. None has been as well-received, both critically and commercially, in recent years as HBO's The Pitt. Following the show's success, Netflix attempted to produce its own alternative, Pulse, which was canceled after a single season. Now, Netflix has delivered a show that seems to have instantly captured global attention following its debut.

According to the streamer's viewership report, which tracks the week of October 5 to October 11, the number-one title on the non-English shows list was the South Korean medical thriller Doctor X: Mafia in White. Like most shows that belong to this genre, the new Korean series revolves around a genius doctor who is regarded as a loose cannon by her peers, and is forced to suffer fools and navigate systemic corruption while performing medical miracles. The new show is based on the Japanese hit Doctor-X: Surgeon Michiko Daimon, which aired for seven seasons between 2012 and 2021.

Collider Exclusive · TV Medicine Quiz
Which Fictional Hospital Would You Work Best In?
The Pitt · ER · Grey's Anatomy · House · Scrubs

Five hospitals. Five completely different ways medicine goes sideways on television — brutal, chaotic, romantic, brilliant, and ridiculous. Only one of them is the ward your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out exactly where you belong.

🚨The Pitt

🏥ER

💉Grey's

🔬House

🩺Scrubs

FIND YOUR HOSPITAL →

01

A critical patient comes through the door. What's your first instinct?
Medicine under pressure reveals who you actually are.

AStay completely present — block everything else out and work through it step by step, right now.
BTriage fast and delegate — get the right people on the right problems immediately.
CTrust my gut and move — I work best when I stop overthinking and just act.
DAsk the question everyone else is ignoring — what's the thing that doesn't fit?
ETake a breath, make a joke to cut the tension, and then get to work — panic helps no one.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

Why did you go into medicine in the first place?
The honest answer says more about you than the one you'd give in an interview.

ABecause I wanted to be where it matters most — right at the edge, when someone's life is actually on the line.
BBecause I wanted to help people — genuinely, one patient at a time, in a system that makes it hard.
CBecause I was drawn to the intensity of it — the stakes, the drama, the feeling of being fully alive.
DBecause medicine is the most interesting puzzle there is — and I needed a problem worth solving.
EBecause I wanted to make a difference — and also, honestly, I didn't know what else to do with my life.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What do you actually want from the people you work with?
Who you want beside you under pressure is who you are.

ACompetence and calm — I need people who don't fall apart when things get bad.
BTrust and reliability — I want to know that when I pass something off, it's handled.
CConnection — I want colleagues who become family, even if that gets complicated.
DIntelligence and the willingness to be challenged — I have no interest in people who just agree with me.
EFriendship — people I actually like spending twelve hours a day with, because those hours are going to happen either way.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

You lose a patient you fought hard to save. How do you carry it?
Every doctor who's worked a long shift has had to answer this question.

AI carry it. All of it. I don't look for ways to put it down — that weight is part of doing this work honestly.
BI process it and move — you have to, or the next patient suffers for the one you just lost.
CI feel it deeply and lean on the people around me — I don't think you're supposed to handle that alone.
DI go back over every decision — not to punish myself, but because I need to understand what I missed.
EI grieve it genuinely, find some way to laugh about something unrelated, and try to be kind to myself — imperfectly.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

How would your colleagues describe the way you work?
Your reputation on the floor is usually more accurate than your self-image.

AIntense and completely present — no small talk during a shift, but exactly who you want there.
BSteady and dependable — not the flashiest in the room but never the one who drops something.
CPassionate and occasionally chaotic — brilliant on the hard cases, prone to drama everywhere else.
DBrilliant and difficult — right more often than anyone else, and everyone knows it, including me.
EWarm and self-deprecating — not the most intimidating presence, but genuinely good at this and easy to like.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

How do you feel about hospital protocol and procedure?
Every institution has rules. What you do with them is a choice.

AProtocol is the floor, not the ceiling — I follow it until the patient needs something it can't provide.
BI respect it — the system is broken in places, but the structure is there for a reason and I work within it.
CI follow it until my instincts tell me not to — and my instincts are usually right, even when they cause problems.
DRules are for people who haven't thought hard enough about when to break them.
EI try to follow it and mostly do — with a few memorable exceptions that still come up in meetings.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

What does this job cost you personally?
Nobody works in medicine without paying a price. What's yours?

AEverything outside these walls — I've given this job my full attention and the rest of my life has gone around it.
BMy idealism, mostly — I came in believing the system could be fixed and I've made a complicated peace with that.
CStability — my personal life has been as chaotic as the OR, and that's not entirely a coincidence.
DMy relationships — I am not easy to know, and the people who've tried to would probably agree.
EMy sense of gravity — I use humour as a coping mechanism, which not everyone appreciates in a hospital.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

At the end of a long shift, what keeps you coming back?
The answer to this question is the most honest thing about you.

AThe fact that it's real — that nothing else I could be doing would matter this much, right now, today.
BThe patients — individual human beings who needed something and got it because I was there.
CThe people I work with — I have walked through impossible things with these people and I'd do it again.
DThe next unsolved case — there's always another puzzle, and I'm not done yet.
EBecause despite everything — the exhaustion, the loss, the absurdity — I actually love this job.

REVEAL MY HOSPITAL →

Your Assignment Has Been Made
You Belong In…

Your answers have pointed to one fictional hospital above all others. This is the ward your instincts, your temperament, and your particular brand of dysfunction were built for.

Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center

The Pitt

You are built for the most unsparing version of emergency medicine television has ever shown — one that puts you inside a single fifteen-hour shift and doesn't let you look away.

You need your work to be real, not romanticised — meaning over drama, honesty over aesthetics.

You find purpose inside the work itself, not in the chaos surrounding it.

You've made peace with the fact that this job takes from you constantly, and gives back in ways that are harder to name.

Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center demands exactly that kind of person — and you would not want to be anywhere else.

County General Hospital, Chicago

ER

You are the person who keeps the whole floor running — not the most brilliant in the room, but possibly the most essential.

You show up, do the work, absorb the losses, and come back the next day without needing the job to be anything other than what it is.

You care about patients as individual human beings, not as cases to solve or dramas to live through.

You believe in the system even when it fails you — and you understand that emergency medicine is about holding the line just long enough.

ER is television about endurance. You have it.

Grey Sloan Memorial Hospital, Seattle

Grey's Anatomy

You came to medicine with your whole self — your ambition, your emotions, your relationships, your history — and you have never quite managed to leave any of it at the door.

You feel things fully and form deep attachments to the people you work with.

Your personal and professional lives are permanently, chaotically entangled — and that entanglement drives both your greatest disasters and your most remarkable saves.

You understand that extraordinary medicine often happens at the intersection of clinical skill and profound human connection.

It's messy at Grey Sloan. You would not have it any other way.

Princeton-Plainsboro Teaching Hospital, NJ

House

You are drawn to the problem above everything else — the symptom that doesn't fit, the diagnosis hiding underneath the obvious one.

You're not primarily motivated by the patient as a person — though you are capable of caring, even if you'd deny it.

You work best when the stakes are highest and the standard answer is wrong.

Princeton-Plainsboro exists to house one extraordinary, impossible mind — and everyone around that mind is there because they're smart enough to keep up.

The only way forward here is to think harder than everyone else in the room. That is exactly what you do.

Sacred Heart Hospital, California

Scrubs

You understand that medicine is tragic and absurd in almost equal measure — and that the only sane response is to hold both of those things at the same time.

You are warm, self-aware, and funnier than most people in your field.

You use humour to get through terrible moments — and at Sacred Heart, that's not a flaw, it's a survival strategy.

You lean on the people around you and let them lean back. The laughter and the grief are genuinely inseparable here.

Scrubs is a show about learning to become someone worthy of the job. You are still very much in the middle of that process — which is exactly right.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

The New Medical Thriller Outperformed Several Holdover Hits

The new Korean version is headlined by Kim Ji-won, who previously starred in the K-dramas My Liberation Notes and Queen of Tears. Doctor X premiered on Korean television on October 9, drawing 2.2 million viewers per Nielsen Korea. The second episode followed on October 10, and drew 2.8 million viewers. According to Netflix, the show amassed 4.6 million views across the world this past week, outperforming the first season of Percy Jackson & the Olympians, as well as holdover hits such as Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, The Gentlemen, and A Different World. Doctor X was the number-one show in seven countries, and among the top 10 in 36 countries. You can check out the first two episodes on Netflix; the next two episodes will air on October 16 and October 17 in South Korea, with the 12th and final episode scheduled for November 14. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

items.text:
"The triple-A industry has become over-specialised, specialised to the point of hyper-fragility," Mark Darrah states in a foreboding interview found deep in the pages of the Summer Eternal Anthology, recently covered by Edwin. As a former executive producer at Bioware, who corralled teams on Anthem and Dragon Age, after starting his career as a programmer on Baldur's Gate, Neverwinter Nights, and Jade Empire, Darrah has seen firsthand the growing scale of video game production and the challenges it can bring.

Darrah's also been vocal about the difficult development of Anthem in the past, and the struggles he had at Bioware. However, while what he says in the interview may be familiar, I found it gained sharper definition when read in light of games industry news and some of the interviews I've had with developers this year. So let me pull together some of the choice bits with the extra context from our own RPS vaults.

I should say, I've not laid hands myself on the Summer Eternal Anthology - a 500-page manifesto/design document/making-of book for Red Rooster, the new RPG from a splinter group of former Disco Elysium developers. But Edwin, who acknowledges that he's acknowledged in the acknowledgements section, did send me some photos of the interview with Darrah that's found deep within its pages.

Anyway, back to the Darrah's warning of over-specialisation. One of the problems, he says, is that it's caused teams to balloon in size because "No one person can add anything into a triple-A game. It requires at least five people." Obviously, the immediate implication of this is that larger teams cost more to run. But Darrah then links the complexity of projects to the increased risk of a delay. "If you have a 500-person team and you go one month late, that's probably adding five, ten million to your budget right there. It doesn't take much. To put that in another context, consider Grand Theft Auto VI. Darrah speculates that the growing complexity may also be encouraging larger studios to stay in the prototyping phase because "prototyping is the one place where the devs are still allowed to be creative, so they don't want to leave that phase because they don't want to get down to just executing lists." Though, as Willits told me, having a fully-staffed team working on a prototype is terrible news for a studio's bottom line – "you do not need 200 people before you have a vertical slice, you're burning money."

Even if a game does come out at the end of that long, expensive production, it now has to earn back significantly more to break even. But, more and more, we're seeing executives get scared of the mounting costs of an in-development game and cutting bait while it's still in the pre-production phase. Just look at Perfect Dark and Everwild.

Darrah touches on the risk of that long, hard-to-leave-behind prototyping phase, because while you want developers to add things to the game "you don't want them to be able to generate work for other people. And as people have gotten more specialised, the ability for people to add things to the game that doesn't generate work for other people is basically vanishingly small."

Threaded through the interview with Darrah is his prediction that the games industry is headed toward a "bifurcation", in which several games will tear away from the rest of the market and become an unreachable target for other publishers, forcing them to scale their expectations down. "GTA 6 is going to rip itself off and take five or six games with it, up into the upper echelon of 'we can spend any amount of money on our games and it's going to be all right,'" Darrah says. Along with Rockstar's crime 'em up, he suggests Assassin's Creed, Call of Duty, and Battlefield could join it. He says there are just too many games that have $100m budgets that aren't making that money back.

Darrah points to his old studio Bioware as an example of one of the victims of this split. "BioWare sat right at the point where it doesn't quite work." Shortly after Dragon Age: Veilguard's launch, EA CEO Andrew Wilson said the RPG had significantly underperformed, reaching only 1.5m players, less than the 3m the company had planned for. (Also, worth noting, that's not 1.5m sales, as the game had a free trial available and was available through EA's subscription service.)

As much as this may sound like something out of Bioshock, with all of the top-selling games breaking away and making a home under the sea where they just eat all of the money for the rest of time, Darrah paints a surprisingly optimistic picture. "If that is happening, then I think you're going to see a lot more studios the size of Sandfall Interactive's Expedition 33. These are teams that are pretty small, pretty focused – Clair Obscur was very small with unusually massive outsourcing – a roughly 40-person team."

Darrah explains that the difference between Sandfall and so many other teams in the industry is that typically a studio has a representative of all the disciplines it needs in-house – designers, artists, programmers, testers, audio people – and outsourcing is used to expand the capacity of the team, providing artists to work with the art director, for instance. But, Darrah says, Sandfall is different. "It looks to me like what Sandfall did was to keep entire holes in their structure – they don't appear to have any internal animators at all, and they outsourced 100% of their animation." The nature of the game, a turn-based RPG, helps with that, but even then that's a case of the developer recognising a significant way to reduce the team's overhead.

(Another example of a studio seemingly outsourcing smartly to keep their headcount low, look at what Neon Giant's achieving with immersive sim No Law.)

I will also point out that, while outsourcing can reduce costs for a studio, for the recipients of the work it can mean low wages and a figurative straitjacket. South American developers told James earlier this year how, despite their evident expertise, it was still difficult to convince publishers they were perfectly capable to leading projects. All to often, they are only contracted to assist American studios on theirs.

If that great schism happens, with publishers giving up their dreams of making the next GTA or the next Call of Duty, it could, Darrah says, reshape the industry. "If that all goes away, then you'll get a bunch of room to make it work with titles that need to sell 3-4 million units," he says. "That's much more attractive. I don't want to be working on something like GTA, where if this thing doesn't sell 50 million units, it's going to lose money. That's insane."

Though, within this prediction there is something a smidge worrying: the future of CD Projekt. Darrah says the Witcher maker has entered that rarefied space of the mega game – "Their games now need to sell 15, 20 million units to make money." And with that capacity for success but also that necessity for success, well, Darrah says, "that's a really dangerous place to be."

Darrah doesn't offer any predictions for The Witcher 4 or Cyberpunk 2's prospects, but I can't help but think of the news in May that there are already twice as many people working on The Witcher 4 than the 240 who worked on The Witcher 3.

As I say, none of what Darrah is saying is new exactly, but when you look at what's been taking place in the last year, it does sound like a move away from the mega budgets of the early 2020s has to be on the cards for all but the very biggest studios, right?

items.text:
James Bond: First Light Officially Returns March 2027

Published Oct 16, 2026, 3:00 AM EDT

Chris is a Gaming Editor at ScreenRant. He has been a professional writer since 2009, and has written for top TV, comics, movie, and video game outlets like Engadget, Polygon, Destructoid, and more. He brings with him an expertise in every game genre, no matter how niche or mainstream.
You may know him as the former Managing/Reviews Editor of Destructoid, where he published hundreds of game reviews across every genre, including MMOs, sports games, and Metroidvanias.
Find Chris on Twitter @_SRChris.

Watching every James Bond movie a while back was a treat. While not all of them are winners, and many are fiercely debated in terms of quality, the sheer number of different takes on the same formula is a thrill to watch unfold. Every Bond actor offers up something different, even Lazenby, who is arguably in the best Bond flick, On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

That said, the Bond mythos has lulls. While the series was on a roll from 1962 to 1989, delivering a movie roughly every two years, there were gaps, even starting with Brosnan.

It took Eon six years to deliver Goldeneye after License to Kill, four years to transition from Brosnan to Craig, and now, it's going on five years, the longest hiatus in Bond history. You won't have to wait that long this time, though. Thanks to an official announcement on YouTube, we're getting a new release in March 2027.

After weeks of speculation and confusion, IO Interactive has finally revealed the release date for 007 First Light on Switch 2: March 18, 2027. It's still a few months away, but fans were worried that the Switch 2 port would be canned altogether, and now it's fully confirmed, with pre-orders live now.

If you've never played 007 First Light before, it features a young Bond, something not really seen in any iteration of the character so far:

"Follow James Bond as a young, resourceful and sometimes reckless recruit in MI6’s training program, and discover an origin story of the world’s most famous spy. After a heroic act, young Naval air crewman James Bond is offered to join the newly revived Double 0 program. But when a mission to stop a rogue agent ends in tragedy, he must join forces with his reluctant mentor Greenway to expose a deep conspiracy and stop a looming coup at the heart of the State."

Nintendo has even provided a first look at the game on Switch 2, and while the fidelity isn't as impressive as on other systems, it seems to run at a stable framerate. There's also a special pre-order bonus for the Switch 2 edition: The Goldeneye Suit. It features the slick suit and tie that Pierce Brosnan wore in the hit film that brought Bond back into the limelight following up Timothy Dalton.

Switch 2 ports don't always fare well in the current climate, and are sometimes delayed or canceled outright. Take Borderlands 4, for instance, which is "paused indefinitely" on the console until Gearbox can figure it out. It's a shame, because plenty of Switch ports run great, and the Switch 2's enhanced tech makes many ports possible that weren't on the original Switch.

Despite its issues, 007 First Light is one of the only James Bond releases in recent years, following 2021's No Time to Die. Currently, Amazon is trying to cast and develop a new Bond for a new generation, and they'll have to do some showstopping stuff to top the financial success of Daniel Craig's run, warts and all.
