items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

Umami is probably one of the most popular Japanese loanwords in English, being used all the time to describe a distinct savory flavor. This term is a relatively recent adoption into the English language, and it’s somewhat new to Japanese as well.

The word was first coined in 1908 when a Japanese scientist used the word to describe the “5th taste,” which is savoriness. In both Japanese and English, umami generally describes the savory flavor you would find in cooked meats, soy sauce, and mushrooms.

8. Dashi　(だし)

No mention of washoku can exclude dashi, stock made from fish or kelp that is used as the base for many Japanese dishes. Dashi is commonly used in English to mean the same thing.

9. Katsu (curry or chicken katsu)　(かつ)

Katsu refers to cutlets of meat that are breaded using panko and deep-fried. The cutlets are usually pork or chicken. Katsu is served with a sauce or with curry. In fact, in some places overseas, katsu curry has become so popular that the term is used to mean all Japanese curry.

10. Panko　(パン粉)

You might have guessed this from the previous entry, but panko is breadcrumbs. They are commonly used in Japanese cooking and the product and the name have crossed over into English-speaking cultures.

The word panko is actually a combination of a loanword that didn’t come from English and the original Japanese word. “Pan” came from the Portuguese language, pao, and ko (粉) is a Japanese word that means “flour” or “dust”.

The biggest difference between panko and standard breadcrumbs is that panko is made from bread without crusts. Panko’s crustless white bread is coarsely ground into airy, large flakes that give fried foods a light, crunchy coating.

11. Amazake (甘酒)

Making the list of words of Japanese origin recently recorded in the Oxford English Dictionary, amazake is a sweet, fermented drink made from rice. Unlike sake, which is also made from rice, amazake is not alcoholic. It literally means sweet (ama) sake.

12. Manga (漫画)

These loanwords are used the same way in English as they are in Japanese. One distinction is that while manga means comics in general in Japan, the term typically means Japanese comics in English.

13. Anime (アニメ)

Probably the most popular loanword used all the time in English is アニメ (anime), which ironically comes from the word “animation” borrowed from English. But in English, “anime” specifically refers to Japanese animation even though in Japanese it refers to all animation. 14. Emoji　(絵文字)

Texting and instant messaging is just not the same without emoji, graphics that help express an emotion when words are just not enough. But the cute, yellow pictogram you’ve been using on your iPhone? The word came from the Japanese language. The kanji 絵 (え) means “picture” and 文字 (もじ) means “character” or “letter.” You might learn some new emoji from the Emojipedia online.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Sport and Martial Arts

Japanese martial arts are known the world over by their Japanese names. These are quite established loanwords, and the sports themselves continue to gain devotees.

15. Judo　(柔道)

Japanese martial arts are well-known throughout the English-speaking world, by their Japanese names. Judo, a defensive martial art, is no exception. The term originates from soft, gentle (柔; juu) and way, road (道; do). Judo is an Olympic event, and practitioners are usually called judoka (柔道家).

When you’re saying the word “judo” in Japanese, remember to elongate the first syllable: Ju-u-dou. In English, however, you can shorten it.

16. Jujutsu　(柔術)

Precursor to judo, this is also a Japanese unarmed martial art. The first part of the term, juu means gentle, just like in judo and the jutsu (術) means skill or art. There are variant spellings in English, including jiu-jitsu or ju-jitsu. It is also the origin of the name of the famous martial art, Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu.

However, historical evidence shows that Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu (BJJ) comes from Judo, but at the time Judo was still being called “Ju-Jutsu,” which is why BJJ has its name today rather than “Brazilian Judo.”

17. Karate　(空手)

Karate is definitely one of those Japanese loanwords that almost feels like it’s always been in English. The term originates from empty (kara) and hand (te), meaning fighting with bare hands. But the history actually gets more interesting.

Karate originates with the indigenous people of Okinawa, who referred to their martial arts as 手(te or tii in Okinawan). But because the Okinawans traded so much with China, Chinese martial arts heavily influenced Karate, so it was initially called “Chinese hand” (唐手), pronounced the same as we know it today. Eventually, after Japan took over Okinawa, the name was changed to 空手 (karate).

18. Kendo　(剣道)

Another Japanese martial art that was simply imported into English, it consists of participants using bamboo swords and wearing protective gear based loosely on samurai armor. Ken means “sword” and do means “way.”

19. Sumo　(相撲)

Often suffixed with ‘wrestling’ in English, sumo means to fight. It’s not just the word that has crossed borders. Many non-Japanese people have succeeded as sumo wrestlers, in what is perceived to be a closed and very traditional world. Check out this quick guide to sumo related terms to learn a bit more about the sport.

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Performing and Literary Arts

From the theater to the page, traditional Japanese performing and literary arts have become well-known in English-speaking cultures.

20. Kabuki　(歌舞伎)

This is a kind of Japanese theater. The Online Etymology Dictionary cites two possible origins of this Japanese loanword. One is that kabuki comes from the verb kabuku, meaning to deviate. The first kabuki performance was given in a shrine by a girl, dressed as a man, which was outside of the norm. The other explanation is that kabuki means ‘art of song and dance,’ from ka (song), bu (dance), and ki (art, skill).

21. Noh　(能)

In Noh theater, performers sing and dance while wearing masks. This loanword comes from the Japanese meaning ‘talent’.

22. Tanka　(短歌)

A poem written using just five lines, tanka means short (tan) song (ka). In English, the poems typically use five lines and 31 syllables, but in Japanese, they are typically written in three lines.

23. Haiku (俳句)

If you’ve heard about haiku, you probably have the impression that it takes immense skill to craft them. These poems are written using a set number of syllables. The haiku consists of three lines, with five syllables in the first line, seven in the second, and five in the third.

Though haiku were originally written in Japanese, English poems following this pattern also go by the same name. Literally meaning light (haikai no) verse (ku), these poems are often about nature.

23. Senryu (川柳)

Senryu is a loanword that refers to another type of Japanese poetry that’s similar to haiku. It tends to talk about people, rather than nature. This form was named after a poet who frequently practiced it.

From business to bedding and natural disasters, Japanese loanwords are used in many areas of life. The following words don’t fall neatly into the categories we have here. But they are still commonly used.

25. Tycoon (大君)

You’ve probably heard this word used a lot with another t-word, tech, as in tech tycoon. Its origins have little do with technology, however. Taikun was the name foreigners gave to the shogun (another loanword) when they came to Japan in the 1800s. Over time, taikun (great lord) became tycoon. Today, the word refers to someone of tremendous wealth and power.

26. Honcho　(班長)

This is another loanword often used alliteratively with head, as in head honcho, meaning leader. The term originates from Japanese han (group) and cho (leader), and was apparently picked up by foreigners in Japan during the second world war.

27. Skosh (少し: Sukoshi)

Have you ever noticed someone saying, “Just a skosh.” Maybe you’re asking if you need to add more salt when you are making soup. This loanword is a shortening of the Japanese sukoshi, meaning a little. It was adopted by the US servicemen when they were stationed in Japan after World War II. It is used in the same way in English and carries the nuance of a really tiny amount.

28. Zen　(善)

This loanword originates from the Japanese school of Zen Buddhism that focuses on meditation. In common use in English, zen means calm and peaceful, and doesn’t explicitly refer to Buddhism.

29. Futon　(布団)

Futon is one of those loanwords that perhaps many people have forgotten is, in fact, a loanword. It’s used to describe a flat mattress that can be rolled up, which is traditional bedding in Japan. However, in English, people refer to couches that have pull-out beds as futons. The fu in this loanword means sheet or cloth, and the ton means group.

30. Ikigai (生きがい)

Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.

32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.

Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.

33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.

34. Kimono (着物)

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. When you’re in Japan, there are cases where you might need to make a phone call in Japanese, whether that’s for making a restaurant reservation, calling for an emergency, or checking on your friend. Here is where you can no longer rely on gestures or reading subtle body language to figure out what the other person is saying. It’s a true test of your Japanese listening comprehension and speaking skills, where you need to respond rather quickly and hold a conversation with just words and phrases you know.

Contrary to popular belief, you should not use moshi moshi all the time. So, let’s break down how phone calls work in Japanese and how you can navigate them with ease and confidence!

A Bit of Japanese Phone Call Etiquette

Japan is known for its polite and sometimes complex etiquette, which can change depending on the level of formality, and this can apply to phone calls. Whenever you answer a call from a business or service, as a general rule, you use polite language, like the です/ます form. When making calls for work, like when speaking to a client or customer, you should always use keigo, formal Japanese conjugations.

So, a big question you might be asking is whether or not you should use もしもし (moshi moshi). This expression is commonly used when answering phone calls between friends, family, and people you’re more comfortable with. You wouldn’t really use もしもし in formal situations like when talking to strangers, service staff, or on work calls.

Japanese phone etiquette is not complicated and generally follows similar patterns of politeness you would observe in English or your native tongue. You should always start the call with a polite greeting and end with a polite expression conveying farewell or appreciation. So, let’s go through how to navigate a call completely in Japanese, step-by-step.

Making Phone Calls in Japanese

The way you make phone calls in Japanese varies depending on whether you are answering or initiating the call, and whether you’re in a formal or casual context. So, let’s go through some common situations where you would be calling in formal contexts (for work and speaking with clients), casual contexts (talking to friends, family, or people you know), and when speaking to services, like making a reservation.

Making Formal Phone Calls in Japanese

When making formal calls, you must always use very polite Japanese, which, of course, starts with a very respectful greeting. Depending on whether you’ve worked with the person you’re calling before or you are calling someone for the first time, the greeting will actually change.

1. Greeting Business Partners or People You Work with Often

Similar to writing business emails in Japanese, the most common formal greeting in phone calls is お世話になっております (Osewa ni natte orimasu) followed by your name and company. You usually use this greeting with people you have worked with in the past.

Example:

お世話になっております。株式会社アイスクリームのロイです。
Osewa ni natte orimasu. Kabushiki geisha aisu kuriimu no roi desu.
Thank you for your constant support. This is Roy from Ice Cream Inc.

However, if you’re calling a colleague, you should use the phrase お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu). It doesn’t have a great English equivalent, but it conveys appreciation for your colleagues’ hard work and is often used as a greeting to fellow co-workers, including on phone calls. Note: you wouldn’t say お世話になっております to colleagues on phone calls.

Example:

お疲れ様です。ロイです。
Otsukaresama desu. Roi desu.
Hello, this is Roy.

2. Greeting Clients or People You Haven’t Met

When it comes to calling clients, customers, or people you just met, you will usually use a greeting that conveys appreciation. You usually thank the person for answering the call with the expression お電話ありがとうございます (odenwa arigatou gozaimasu), meaning “thank you for the call.”

Example:

お電話ありがとうございます。株式会社アイスクリームのロイでございます。
Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Kabushiki gaisha aisu kuriimu no roi degozaimasu.
Thank you very much for letting me call. This is Roy from Ice Cream Inc.

3. Answering Phone Calls in Formal Situations

When answering a phone call in a business or work capacity, you use extra-polite language known as humble and honorific forms. So, when you receive a call, it’s common to say はい、〜です (hai, ~ desu), meaning “yes, this is…” This is a very polite way to answer a call while also immediately introducing yourself so the caller knows who they are speaking to.

Example:

はい、ロイです。
Hai, roi desu.
Yes, this is Roy speaking.

To make the phrase even more formal, you can change です to its humble form: 〜でございます (degozaimasu). This phrase is very common when answering the phone in work situations.

Example:

はい、株式会社アイスクリームのロイでございます。
Hai, kabushiki gaisha aisu kuriimu no roi degozaimasu.
Hello, this is Roy speaking from Ice Cream Inc.

So, after the caller introduces themselves, if you’re receiving a call from a client company, even if you don’t know the caller directly, you can follow up with the phrase お世話になっております (osewa ni natte orimasu).

4. Asking to Talk to Someone Else

It’s quite common when you’re trying to contact somebody on their work phone number that you will end up calling a department desk, which directs the call to whoever is available. So, if you want to get in contact with a specific person, here is how you can do that.

Example:

すみません、山田さんがいらっしゃいますでしょうか？話させて頂いてよろしいでしょうか？
Sumimasen, Yamada-san ga irashaimasudeshouka? Hanasasete itadaite yoroshii deshouka?
Excuse me, is Yamada-san available? May I speak with him?

5. Scheduling a Meeting

Scheduling a meeting is one of the most common reasons to make a formal phone call in Japanese. Since you’re asking for someone’s valuable time, you’ll want to use polite, humble language to make your request sound considerate and professional.

A common, professional phrase for “meeting” or “discussion” is 打ち合わせ (uchiawase). It’s the everyday business word for a meeting with a client or colleague, and it’s often written with the honorific prefix お to become お打ち合わせ (o-uchiawase) when talking about the other person’s time. 日程 (nittei) means “schedule” or “dates,” and 調整 (chousei) means “to adjust” or “to arrange.” Together with させていただきたいのですが, a humble way of saying “I would like to,” the phrase softly opens the conversation without sounding demanding.

Example:

お打ち合わせの日程を調整させていただきたいのですが、ご都合のよろしい日はございますか？
O uchiawase no nittei o chousei sasete itadakitai no desu ga, gotsugou no yoroshii hi wa gozaimasu ka?
I would like to arrange a time for us to meet. Is there a day that works well for you?

6. When You Can’t Hear the Other Person

Call reception often varies, so it can be hard to hear people. How do you communicate respectfully that you can’t hear someone you’re on the phone with? You can always use one of the most useful Japanese phrases: もう一度お願いします (mou ichido onegaishimasu), which means “one more time, please.” It works as a respectful way to ask someone to repeat themselves for both in-person and over-the-phone interactions.

Example:

すみません、もう一度お願いします。
Sumimasen, mou ichido onegaishimasu.
Excuse me, can you say it one more time, please?

If you want to ask someone if they can hear you, the phrase 聞こえますか？ (kikoe masuka?) works perfectly for this. On business calls, to amp up the politeness, you can say 聞こえますでしょうか？ (kikou masudeshouka?). Adding でしょうか？ (deshouka?) softens the whole expression and works well when you want to show greater respect.

Example:

すみません、聞こえますでしょうか？
Sumimasen, kikoemasu deshouka?
Excuse me, are you able to hear me?

7. Saying Farewell in Formal Calls

Whenever you’re talking with someone who isn’t your family or friends, whether it’s for work, to inquire about a service, or talk to a teacher or coach, you almost always end the call with 失礼します (shitsureishimasu).

It literally means “I’m being rude”. But despite its apologetic nuance, it’s used as a polite way to say goodbye, kind of like saying I’m sorry for hanging up.” You usually say it right before you or the person you’re speaking to ends the call.

Example:

失礼します。
Shitsurei shimasu.
Goodbye.

In formal work calls, it’s common to end the call with a polite expression that conveys a sense of appreciation and desire to work together again. よろしくお願いします (Yoroshiku Onegaishimasu) is one of the most common phrases you can use to end a formal call.

Example:

よろしくお願いします。失礼します。
Yoroshiku onegaishimasu. Shitsureishimasu.
I look forward to working/speaking with you again. Goodbye.

When responding to よろしくお願いします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), it’s very common to say こちらこそよろしくお願いします (kochira koso yoroshiku onegaishimasu), meaning “No, I’m the one who is looking forward to working with you again”. The phrase こちらこそ (kochira koso) is great for expressing a sense of humility and respect for the one other person by putting the responsibility or appreciation on your side.

Making Phone Calls To Friends, Family, and People You Know

When calling friends, family, and people you know, you can drop some of the formalities and use more casual language. But similar to formal calls, greetings tend to change when answering or initiating a phone call. So, let’s break down how to make phone calls in a more casual context.

8. Answering or Starting a Call

もしもし (moshi moshi) is the classic phone greeting in Japanese, and you’ll use it with friends, family, and people you’re comfortable with. It works much like “hello?” in English, and you can use it both when you answer a call and when you start one. It’s also handy if the connection is bad and you want to check that the other person can still hear you.

When answering a call from someone you know, you can simply say もしもし, or add a bit more, like their name or a quick “hey.” If you’re the one calling, it’s polite to say who you are right after.

Example:

もしもし、ケンです。今、大丈夫？
Moshi moshi, Ken desu. Ima, daijoubu?
Hello, it’s Ken. Is now a good time?

Keep in mind that you’d skip もしもし on formal or work calls, where you’d use the greetings from the previous section instead.

9. Checking if They Have Time to Talk

Even in casual calls, it’s good manners to check whether the other person is free before you jump into your reason for calling. Calls can interrupt someone on a train, at work, or in the middle of dinner, so a quick check shows consideration. 今 (ima) means “now,” and 大丈夫 (daijoubu) means “okay” or “alright,” so together they ask “is now okay?”

With people you’re closer with, you can keep it short. With someone a bit older or less familiar, add です/ます to keep things polite.

Example:

もしもし、今ちょっと話せる？
Moshi moshi, ima chotto hanaseru?
Hello, can you talk for a bit right now?

Example 2:

今、お時間大丈夫ですか？
Ima, ojikan daijoubu desu ka?
Do you have a moment right now?

If the other person is busy, you might hear them say 今ちょっと無理 (ima chotto muri), meaning “I can’t right now,” or 後でかけ直すね (ato de kakenaosu ne), meaning “I’ll call you back later.” This is a good phrase to recognize since it’s very common.

10. Making Plans With Friends

One of the most common reasons to call a friend is to make plans, whether it’s grabbing food, going to a movie, or just hanging out. In casual Japanese, the easiest way to invite someone is by using the negative question form 〜しない？ (~shinai?), which literally asks “won’t you ~?” but is actually a friendly way of saying “want to ~?” It sounds much softer and more natural than a direct question.

For more casual invitations, you can also use the volitional form 〜しよう (~shiyou), meaning “let’s ~.”

Example:

今週末、ご飯食べに行かない？
Konshuu matsu, gohan tabe ni ikanai?
Want to go eat this weekend?

Example 2:

じゃあ、土曜日の夜に渋谷で会おう！
Jaa, doyoubi no yoru ni Shibuya de aou!
Then, let’s meet in Shibuya on Saturday night!

If they say yes, you might hear うん、いいね！ (un, ii ne!), meaning “yeah, sounds good!” If they’re not free, they may say ごめん、その日は予定がある (gomen, sono hi wa yotei ga aru), meaning “sorry, I have plans that day.”

11. Ending a Casual Call

Just like in formal calls, you’ll want to end the conversation politely. The difference is that casual goodbyes are much shorter and more relaxed. また (mata) means “again,” and ね (ne) adds a friendly tone, so またね literally means “see you again!” You can also say じゃあね (jaa ne), another very common way to say “bye for now” among friends.

Before hanging up, it’s common to thank them for their time or confirm your plans one more time.

Example:

じゃあ、また明日ね！
Jaa, mata ashita ne!
Well then, see you tomorrow!

Example 2:

電話ありがとう！またね。
Denwa arigatou! Mata ne.
Thanks for calling! Talk to you later.

If you’re talking to someone a bit older or more distant, you can swap in a more polite option like 失礼します (shitsurei shimasu), which is the standard way to end a call politely, or ありがとうございました (arigatou gozaimashita).

Making Phone Calls to Service Staff in Japanese

Phone calls to service staff are more formal than calls to friends or family, but you don’t need to employ the same level of keigo when making calls at work. You also don’t really need to say formal greetings, since the service staff will immediately introduce themselves and ask how they can help you. So, all you really need to do is go straight to the point and respond.

12. Calling to Make a Reservation

Making a reservation in Japanese on the phone is relatively straightforward. You just state you’re calling to make a reservation and then the staff will ask follow-up questions to get your name under which the reservation will be made, the number of people, and time. Let’s take a look at a general phone call to make a reservation.
Example:

(You dial the restaurant number to call)

スタッフ：お電話ありがとうございます。ベストタコスです。
Sutaffu: Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Besuto Takosu desu.
Staff: Thank you for calling. This is Best Tacos.

あなた：すみません、今日の午後9時に5人で予約をしたいのですが。
Anata: Sumimasen, kyou no gogo kuji ni gonin de yoyaku o shitai no desu ga.
You: Excuse me, I would like to make a reservation for 5 people at 9 p.m. today.

スタッフ：本日9時に5名様でご予約でよろしいでしょうか？お席を確認いたしますので、少々お待ちください。
Sutaffu: Honjitsu kuji ni gomeisama de goyoyaku de yoroshii deshouka? Oseki o kakunin itashimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
Staff: A reservation for 5 people at 9 p.m. today, correct? Please wait a moment while I check if seats are available.

あなた：はい、お願いします。
Anata: Hai, onegaishimasu.
You: Yes, please.

スタッフ：お待たせしました。お席をご用意できます。お名前とお電話番号をお伺いしてもよろしいでしょうか？
Sutaffu: Omatase shimashita. Oseki o goyoui dekimasu. Onamae to odenwa bangou o oukagai shitemo yoroshii deshouka?
Staff: Thank you for waiting. We can prepare a table for you. May I have your name and phone number?

あなた：ロイと申します。電話番号は090-1234-5678です。
Anata: Roi to moushimasu. Denwa bangou wa zero kyuu zero no ichi ni san yon no go roku nana hachi desu.
You: My name is Roy. My phone number is 090-1234-5678.

スタッフ：ご予約ありがとうございます。ロイ様、9時に5名様でお待ちしております。
Sutaffu: Goyoyaku arigatou gozaimasu. Roi-sama, kuji ni gomeisama de omachi shite orimasu.
Staff: Thank you for your reservation. Roy, we look forward to seeing your party of 5 at 9 p.m.

あなた：ありがとうございます。失礼します。
Anata: Arigatou gozaimasu. Shitsurei shimasu.
You: Thank you. Goodbye.

スタッフ：失礼いたします。
Sutaffu: Shitsurei itashimasu.
Staff: Goodbye.

13. Calling for a Delivery

One of the most common reasons you may need to call a service person is to reschedule a delivery. Usually, when you miss a delivery, you will find a notice slip in your mailbox with the phrase 再配達 (saihaitatsu), which means “redelivery.” Many companies also let you request it through an app or website.

On the slip or website, you will also find your package’s お問い合わせ番号 (Otoiawase bangou), which translates to “inquiry number.” There’s usually a phone number on the slip or website, and when you call it, the staff will ask for the inquiry number so they can easily identify your package and proceed with redelivering it.

So, here is how you can call the delivery company or driver to redeliver a package.

Example:

(You call the delivery company to reschedule a missed delivery)

スタッフ：お電話ありがとうございます。ジャパン宅配でございます。
Sutaffu: Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Japan Takuhai de gozaimasu.
Staff: Thank you for calling. This is Japan Delivery.

あなた：お世話になっております。荷物の再配達をお願いしたいのですが。
Anata: Osewa ni natte orimasu. Nimotsu no saihaitatsu o onegai shitai no desu ga.
You: Thank you for your support. I would like to request a redelivery of a package.

スタッフ：かしこまりました。お問い合わせ番号をお伺いしてもよろしいでしょうか？
Sutaffu: Kashikomarimashita. Otoiawase bangou o oukagai shitemo yoroshii deshouka?
Staff: Certainly. May I have your inquiry number?

あなた：はい、1234-5678-9012です。
Anata: Hai, ichi ni san yon no go roku nana hachi no kyuu zero ichi ni desu.
You: Yes, it’s 1234-5678-9012.

スタッフ：ありがとうございます。確認いたしますので、少々お待ちください。
Sutaffu: Arigatou gozaimasu. Kakunin itashimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
Staff: Thank you. Please wait a moment while I check.

スタッフ：お待たせいたしました。ご希望のお届け時間はございますか？
Sutaffu: Omatase itashimashita. Gokibou no otodoke jikan wa gozaimasu ka?
Staff: Thank you for waiting. Do you have a preferred delivery time?

あなた：今日の夜7時から9時の間でお願いできますか？
Anata: Kyou no yoru shichiji kara kuji no aida de onegai dekimasu ka?
You: Could you deliver between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. tonight?

スタッフ：かしこまりました。本日19時から21時の間にお届けいたします。
Sutaffu: Kashikomarimashita. Honjitsu juukuji kara nijuuichiji no aida ni otodoke itashimasu.
Staff: Understood. We will deliver it between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. today.

あなた：よろしくお願いします。失礼します。
Anata: Yoroshiku onegai shimasu. Shitsurei shimasu.
You: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

スタッフ：失礼いたします。
Sutaffu: Shitsurei itashimasu.
Staff: Goodbye.

Conclusion: Making Phone Calls in Japanese is Easier than You Think

Making a phone call in Japanese can seem daunting because you need to understand everything the caller is saying and respond in Japanese without relying on gestures or anything else you can use in person. But knowing just a few Japanese phrases can allow you to hold a phone call completely in Japanese, from making a reservation to making plans.

FAQ:

When should I use もしもし (moshi moshi) on the phone?

Use it when answering calls from friends, family, or people you’re comfortable with. Skip it on formal calls, like those with clients, service staff, or coworkers, where you’d use greetings like お世話になっております or はい、〜でございます instead.

How do I greet someone on a business call in Japanese?

お世話になっております (osewa ni natte orimasu) is the standard greeting for people you’ve worked with before, followed by your name and company. For first-time contacts or customers, お電話ありがとうございます (odenwa arigatou gozaimasu) is the usual choice.

How do I ask to speak with a specific person?

Use a polite phrase like 山田さんはいらっしゃいますでしょうか？ (Yamada-san wa irasshaimasu deshouka?), meaning “Is Mr. Yamada available?” Adding 話させていただいてよろしいでしょうか (may I speak with him?) makes it even more polite.

Do I need to use keigo when calling a restaurant or delivery company?

Yes, it’s best to use polite Japanese. Phrases like 予約をしたいのですが (I’d like to make a reservation) and 〜をお願いしたいのですが (I’d like to request ~) sound natural and respectful, and staff will typically respond in keigo.

How do I end a phone call politely in Japanese?

失礼します (shitsurei shimasu) is the standard polite way to end a call, and it works in both formal and service situations. With friends and family, a casual またね (mata ne) or じゃあね (jaa ne) is perfectly fine.

Thank you for your constant support. This is Roy from Ice Cream Inc.

However, if you’re calling a colleague, you should use the phrase お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu). It doesn’t have a great English equivalent, but it conveys appreciation for your colleagues’ hard work and is often used as a greeting to fellow co-workers, including on phone calls. Note: you wouldn’t say お世話になっております to colleagues on phone calls.
Example:

お疲れ様です。ロイです。
Otsukaresama desu. Roi desu.
Hello, this is Roy.
2. Greeting Clients or People You Haven’t Met

When it comes to calling clients, customers, or people you just met, you will usually use a greeting that conveys appreciation. You usually thank the person for answering the call with the expression お電話ありがとうございます (odenwa arigatou gozaimasu), meaning “thank you for the call.”
Example:

お電話ありがとうございます。株式会社アイスクリームのロイでございます。
Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Kabushiki gaisha aisu kuriimu no roi degozaimasu.
Thank you very much for letting me call. This is Roy from Ice Cream Inc.
3. Answering Phone Calls in Formal Situations

When answering a phone call in a business or work capacity, you use extra-polite language known as humble and honorific forms. So, when you receive a call, it’s common to say はい、〜です (hai, ~ desu), meaning “yes, this is…” This is a very polite way to answer a call while also immediately introducing yourself so the caller knows who they are speaking to.
Example:

はい、ロイです。
Hai, roi desu.
Yes, this is Roy speaking.
To make the phrase even more formal, you can change です to its humble form: 〜でございます (degozaimasu). This phrase is very common when answering the phone in work situations.
Example:

はい、株式会社アイスクリームのロイでございます。
Hai, kabushiki gaisha aisu kuriimu no roi degozaimasu.
Hello, this is Roy speaking from Ice Cream Inc.

So, after the caller introduces themselves, if you’re receiving a call from a client company, even if you don’t know the caller directly, you can follow up with the phrase お世話になっております (osewa ni natte orimasu).
4. Asking to Talk to Someone Else

It’s quite common when you’re trying to contact somebody on their work phone number that you will end up calling a department desk, which directs the call to whoever is available. So, if you want to get in contact with a specific person, here is how you can do that.
Example:

すみません、山田さんがいらっしゃいますでしょうか？話させて頂いてよろしいでしょうか？
Sumimasen, Yamada-san ga irashaimasudeshouka? Hanasasete itadaite yoroshii deshouka?
Excuse me, is Yamada-san available? May I speak with him?
5. Scheduling a Meeting

Scheduling a meeting is one of the most common reasons to make a formal phone call in Japanese. Since you’re asking for someone’s valuable time, you’ll want to use polite, humble language to make your request sound considerate and professional.

A common, professional phrase for “meeting” or “discussion” is 打ち合わせ (uchiawase). It’s the everyday business word for a meeting with a client or colleague, and it’s often written with the honorific prefix お to become お打ち合わせ (o-uchiawase) when talking about the other person’s time. 日程 (nittei) means “schedule” or “dates,” and 調整 (chousei) means “to adjust” or “to arrange.” Together with させていただきたいのですが, a humble way of saying “I would like to,” the phrase softly opens the conversation without sounding demanding.
Example:

お打ち合わせの日程を調整させていただきたいのですが、ご都合のよろしい日はございますか？
O uchiawase no nittei o chousei sasete itadakitai no desu ga, gotsugou no yoroshii hi wa gozaimasu ka?
I would like to arrange a time for us to meet. Is there a day that works well for you?
6. When You Can’t Hear the Other Person

Call reception often varies, so it can be hard to hear people. How do you communicate respectfully that you can’t hear someone you’re on the phone with? You can always use one of the most useful Japanese phrases: もう一度お願いします (mou ichido onegaishimasu), which means “one more time, please.” It works as a respectful way to ask someone to repeat themselves for both in-person and over-the-phone interactions.
Example:

すみません、もう一度お願いします。
Sumimasen, mou ichido onegaishimasu.
Excuse me, can you say it one more time, please?

If you want to ask someone if they can hear you, the phrase 聞こえますか？ (kikoe masuka?) works perfectly for this. On business calls, to amp up the politeness, you can say 聞こえますでしょうか？ (kikou masudeshouka?). Adding でしょうか？ (deshouka?) softens the whole expression and works well when you want to show greater respect.
Example:

すみません、聞こえますでしょうか？
Sumimasen, kikoemasu deshouka?
Excuse me, are you able to hear me?
7. Saying Farewell in Formal Calls

Whenever you’re talking with someone who isn’t your family or friends, whether it’s for work, to inquire about a service, or talk to a teacher or coach, you almost always end the call with 失礼します (shitsureishimasu).

It literally means “I’m being rude”. But despite its apologetic nuance, it’s used as a polite way to say goodbye, kind of like saying I’m sorry for hanging up.” You usually say it right before you or the person you’re speaking to ends the call.
Example:

失礼します。
Shitsurei shimasu.
Goodbye.

In formal work calls, it’s common to end the call with a polite expression that conveys a sense of appreciation and desire to work together again. よろしくお願いします (Yoroshiku Onegaishimasu) is one of the most common phrases you can use to end a formal call.
Example:

よろしくお願いします。失礼します。
Yoroshiku onegaishimasu. Shitsureishimasu.
I look forward to working/speaking with you again. Goodbye.

When responding to よろしくお願いします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), it’s very common to say こちらこそよろしくお願いします (kochira koso yoroshiku onegaishimasu), meaning “No, I’m the one who is looking forward to working with you again”. The phrase こちらこそ (kochira koso) is great for expressing a sense of humility and respect for the one other person by putting the responsibility or appreciation on your side.
Making Phone Calls To Friends, Family, and People You Know

When calling friends, family, and people you know, you can drop some of the formalities and use more casual language. But similar to formal calls, greetings tend to change when answering or initiating a phone call. So, let’s break down how to make phone calls in a more casual context.
8. Answering or Starting a Call

もしもし (moshi moshi) is the classic phone greeting in Japanese, and you’ll use it with friends, family, and people you’re comfortable with. It works much like “hello?” in English, and you can use it both when you answer a call and when you start one. It’s also handy if the connection is bad and you want to check that the other person can still hear you.
When answering a call from someone you know, you can simply say もしもし, or add a bit more, like their name or a quick “hey.” If you’re the one calling, it’s polite to say who you are right after.
Example:

もしもし、ケンです。今、大丈夫？
Moshi moshi, Ken desu. Ima, daijoubu?
Hello, it’s Ken. Is now a good time?
Keep in mind that you’d skip もしもし on formal or work calls, where you’d use the greetings from the previous section instead.
9. Checking if They Have Time to Talk

Even in casual calls, it’s good manners to check whether the other person is free before you jump into your reason for calling. Calls can interrupt someone on a train, at work, or in the middle of dinner, so a quick check shows consideration. 今 (ima) means “now,” and 大丈夫 (daijoubu) means “okay” or “alright,” so together they ask “is now okay?”
With people you’re closer with, you can keep it short. With someone a bit older or less familiar, add です/ます to keep things polite.
Example:

もしもし、今ちょっと話せる？
Moshi moshi, ima chotto hanaseru?
Hello, can you talk for a bit right now?
Example 2:

今、お時間大丈夫ですか？
Ima, ojikan daijoubu desu ka?
Do you have a moment right now?

If the other person is busy, you might hear them say 今ちょっと無理 (ima chotto muri), meaning “I can’t right now,” or 後でかけ直すね (ato de kakenaosu ne), meaning “I’ll call you back later.” This is a good phrase to recognize since it’s very common.
10. Making Plans With Friends

One of the most common reasons to call a friend is to make plans, whether it’s grabbing food, going to a movie, or just hanging out. In casual Japanese, the easiest way to invite someone is by using the negative question form 〜しない？ (~shinai?), which literally asks “won’t you ~?” but is actually a friendly way of saying “want to ~?” It sounds much softer and more natural than a direct question.
For more casual invitations, you can also use the volitional form 〜しよう (~shiyou), meaning “let’s ~.”
Example:

今週末、ご飯食べに行かない？
Konshuu matsu, gohan tabe ni ikanai?
Want to go eat this weekend?
Example 2:

じゃあ、土曜日の夜に渋谷で会おう！
Jaa, doyoubi no yoru ni Shibuya de aou!
Then, let’s meet in Shibuya on Saturday night!

If they say yes, you might hear うん、いいね！ (un, ii ne!), meaning “yeah, sounds good!” If they’re not free, they may say ごめん、その日は予定がある (gomen, sono hi wa yotei ga aru), meaning “sorry, I have plans that day.”
11. Ending a Casual Call

Just like in formal calls, you’ll want to end the conversation politely. The difference is that casual goodbyes are much shorter and more relaxed. また (mata) means “again,” and ね (ne) adds a friendly tone, so またね literally means “see you again!” You can also say じゃあね (jaa ne), another very common way to say “bye for now” among friends.
Before hanging up, it’s common to thank them for their time or confirm your plans one more time.
Example:

じゃあ、また明日ね！
Jaa, mata ashita ne!
Well then, see you tomorrow!
Example 2:

電話ありがとう！またね。
Denwa arigatou! Mata ne.
Thanks for calling! Talk to you later.

If you’re talking to someone a bit older or more distant, you can swap in a more polite option like 失礼します (shitsurei shimasu), which is the standard way to end a call politely, or ありがとうございました (arigatou gozaimashita).
Making Phone Calls to Service Staff in Japanese

Phone calls to service staff are more formal than calls to friends or family, but you don’t need to employ the same level of keigo when making calls at work. You also don’t really need to say formal greetings, since the service staff will immediately introduce themselves and ask how they can help you. So, all you really need to do is go straight to the point and respond.
12. Calling to Make a Reservation

Making a reservation in Japanese on the phone is relatively straightforward. You just state you’re calling to make a reservation and then the staff will ask follow-up questions to get your name under which the reservation will be made, the number of people, and time. Let’s take a look at a general phone call to make a reservation.
Example:
(You dial the restaurant number to call)

スタッフ：お電話ありがとうございます。ベストタコスです。
Sutaffu: Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Besuto Takosu desu.
Staff: Thank you for calling. This is Best Tacos.

あなた：すみません、今日の午後9時に5人で予約をしたいのですが。
Anata: Sumimasen, kyou no gogo kuji ni gonin de yoyaku o shitai no desu ga.
You: Excuse me, I would like to make a reservation for 5 people at 9 p.m. today.

スタッフ：本日9時に5名様でご予約でよろしいでしょうか？お席を確認いたしますので、少々お待ちください。
Sutaffu: Honjitsu kuji ni gomeisama de goyoyaku de yoroshii deshouka? Oseki o kakunin itashimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
Staff: A reservation for 5 people at 9 p.m. today, correct? Please wait a moment while I check if seats are available.

あなた：はい、お願いします。
Anata: Hai, onegaishimasu.
You: Yes, please.

スタッフ：お待たせしました。お席をご用意できます。お名前とお電話番号をお伺いしてもよろしいでしょうか？
Sutaffu: Omatase shimashita. Oseki o goyoui dekimasu. Onamae to odenwa bangou o oukagai shitemo yoroshii deshouka?
Staff: Thank you for waiting. We can prepare a table for you. May I have your name and phone number?

あなた：ロイと申します。電話番号は090-1234-5678です。
Anata: Roi to moushimasu. Denwa bangou wa zero kyuu zero no ichi ni san yon no go roku nana hachi desu.
You: My name is Roy. My phone number is 090-1234-5678.

スタッフ：ご予約ありがとうございます。ロイ様、9時に5名様でお待ちしております。
Sutaffu: Goyoyaku arigatou gozaimasu. Roi-sama, kuji ni gomeisama de omachi shite orimasu.
Staff: Thank you for your reservation. Roy, we look forward to seeing your party of 5 at 9 p.m.

あなた：ありがとうございます。失礼します。
Anata: Arigatou gozaimasu. Shitsurei shimasu.
You: Thank you. Goodbye.

スタッフ：失礼いたします。
Sutaffu: Shitsurei itashimasu.
Staff: Goodbye.
13. Calling for a Delivery

One of the most common reasons you may need to call a service person is to reschedule a delivery. Usually, when you miss a delivery, you will find a notice slip in your mailbox with the phrase 再配達 (saihaitatsu), which means “redelivery.” Many companies also let you request it through an app or website.

On the slip or website, you will also find your package’s お問い合わせ番号 (Otoiawase bangou), which translates to “inquiry number.” There’s usually a phone number on the slip or website, and when you call it, the staff will ask for the inquiry number so they can easily identify your package and proceed with redelivering it.
So, here is how you can call the delivery company or driver to redeliver a package.
Example:
(You call the delivery company to reschedule a missed delivery)

スタッフ：お電話ありがとうございます。ジャパン宅配でございます。
Sutaffu: Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Japan Takuhai de gozaimasu.
Staff: Thank you for calling. This is Japan Delivery.

あなた：お世話になっております。荷物の再配達をお願いしたいのですが。
Anata: Osewa ni natte orimasu. Nimotsu no saihaitatsu o onegai shitai no desu ga.
You: Thank you for your support. I would like to request a redelivery of a package.

スタッフ：かしこまりました。お問い合わせ番号をお伺いしてもよろしいでしょうか？
Sutaffu: Kashikomarimashita. Otoiawase bangou o oukagai shitemo yoroshii deshouka?
Staff: Certainly. May I have your inquiry number?

あなた：はい、1234-5678-9012です。
Anata: Hai, ichi ni san yon no go roku nana hachi no kyuu zero ichi ni desu.
You: Yes, it’s 1234-5678-9012.

スタッフ：ありがとうございます。確認いたしますので、少々お待ちください。
Sutaffu: Arigatou gozaimasu. Kakunin itashimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
Staff: Thank you. Please wait a moment while I check.

スタッフ：お待たせいたしました。ご希望のお届け時間はございますか？
Sutaffu: Omatase itashimashita. Gokibou no otodoke jikan wa gozaimasu ka?
Staff: Thank you for waiting. Do you have a preferred delivery time?

あなた：今日の夜7時から9時の間でお願いできますか？
Anata: Kyou no yoru shichiji kara kuji no aida de onegai dekimasu ka?
You: Could you deliver between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. tonight?

スタッフ：かしこまりました。本日19時から21時の間にお届けいたします。
Sutaffu: Kashikomarimashita. Honjitsu juukuji kara nijuuichiji no aida ni otodoke itashimasu.
Staff: Understood. We will deliver it between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. today.

あなた：よろしくお願いします。失礼します。
Anata: Yoroshiku onegai shimasu. Shitsurei shimasu.
You: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

スタッフ：失礼いたします。
Sutaffu: Shitsurei itashimasu.
Staff: Goodbye.
Conclusion: Making Phone Calls in Japanese is Easier than You Think

Making a phone call in Japanese can seem daunting because you need to understand everything the caller is saying and respond in Japanese without relying on gestures or anything else you can use in person. But knowing just a few Japanese phrases can allow you to hold a phone call completely in Japanese, from making a reservation to making plans.

If you want to build confidence to take phone calls completely in Japanese, then join us at Coto Academy! Our courses focus on practical Japanese conversational skills that you can use in your daily life, whether it’s for phone calls, ordering food, or even working in Japan.

So, visit one of our campuses in Tokyo and Yokohama, or join us online from anywhere around the world! Ready to sign up or just want to have a casual chat to learn more details? Just fill out the form below!
FAQ:
When should I use もしもし (moshi moshi) on the phone?

Use it when answering calls from friends, family, or people you’re comfortable with. Skip it on formal calls, like those with clients, service staff, or coworkers, where you’d use greetings like お世話になっております or はい、〜でございます instead.
How do I greet someone on a business call in Japanese?

お世話になっております (osewa ni natte orimasu) is the standard greeting for people you’ve worked with before, followed by your name and company. For first-time contacts or customers, お電話ありがとうございます (odenwa arigatou gozaimasu) is the usual choice.
How do I ask to speak with a specific person?
Use a polite phrase like 山田さんはいらっしゃいますでしょうか？ (Yamada-san wa irasshaimasu deshouka?), meaning “Is Mr. Yamada available?” Adding 話させていただいてよろしいでしょうか (may I speak with him?) makes it even more polite.
Do I need to use keigo when calling a restaurant or delivery company?

Yes, it’s best to use polite Japanese. Phrases like 予約をしたいのですが (I’d like to make a reservation) and 〜をお願いしたいのですが (I’d like to request ~) sound natural and respectful, and staff will typically respond in keigo.
How do I end a phone call politely in Japanese?

失礼します (shitsurei shimasu) is the standard polite way to end a call, and it works in both formal and service situations. With friends and family, a casual またね (mata ne) or じゃあね (jaa ne) is perfectly fine.

When a 50-year-old bar owner in Osaka came home one day last year, he discovered that his wife of more than 20 years had moved out. She had taken her belongings without explicitly telling him she wanted a divorce. Now, he told Kansai TV, the apartment feels empty, the laundry piles up and he eats dinner alone. Looking back on their marriage, he wonders whether he should have paid more attention to how she was feeling.

His experience comes amid renewed attention to jukunen rikon, Japan’s term for late-life divorce. According to government statistics reported by Kansai TV on October 13, couples married for at least 20 years now account for a record 24% of divorces, even as the total number of divorces has declined since its 2002 peak. Divorce counselor Atsuko Okano estimates that women initiate 70% to 80% of the late-life separations she encounters, a figure drawn from her own practice rather than national data.

A 1960s advertisement for a washer, text reads “New model released!”

The Making of the Japanese Housewife

The sengyo shufu, or full-time housewife, is often treated as a fixture of traditional Japanese family life, although the household arrangement associated with her is largely a product of the country’s modern economy. In agricultural communities, women had long worked alongside their families, but the expansion of salaried employment, especially during the postwar economic boom, allowed more households to depend on a husband’s earnings.

By 1980, Japanese households with a working husband and stay-at-home wife outnumbered dual-income households by nearly two to one, according to government labor statistics. The husband devoted himself to his company, often working long hours and socializing with colleagues afterward, while his wife managed the household and raised the children. She might also be expected to care for his aging parents, an obligation with roots in Japan’s prewar ie family system, which placed particular responsibilities on women marrying into their husbands’ families.

The economic bubble burst, more married women entered paid employment and dual-income households eventually outnumbered single-earner ones, although much of the housework and caregiving remained women’s responsibility. For couples who spent decades following these routines, retirement could be a difficult adjustment. A husband who was once at the office for most of the day is suddenly home, often expecting the same domestic attention, while his wife finds herself reorganizing a daily life she had long been accustomed to managing on her own.

Still from the the 2005 TV Asahi drama Jukunen Rikon | © TV Asahi

Retired Husband Syndrome

A 2021 study of nearly 4,000 Japanese women found that their psychological distress increased modestly after their husbands retired. The phenomenon is sometimes called “retired husband syndrome,” though Japanese wives have come up with rather more colorful descriptions. Nure ochiba, or “wet fallen leaves,” describes husbands who follow their wives everywhere, clinging to them like damp leaves that cling to a broom no matter how much you sweep. Sodai gomi, literally “bulky garbage,” refers to husbands who spend their retirement taking up space around the house. The former was popularized by women’s advocate Keiko Higuchi, who recalled first hearing the comparison from a housewife in 1981.

The idea of wives leaving their husbands at retirement was already familiar enough to become prime-time entertainment. In the 2005 TV Asahi drama Jukunen Rikon, a newly retired salaryman buys his wife a ¥120,000 diamond ring and starts planning their holidays, only for her to announce, at his retirement dinner, that she wants a divorce. He overturns the dinner table. The series was a surprise hit, particularly among women over 40, and inspired a wave of magazine articles offering advice to husbands worried they might be next.

The Pension Reform Men Feared

In 2006, while conducting fieldwork in Japan, anthropologist Allison Alexy met a middle-aged man who became visibly nervous upon learning that she studied divorce. A pension reform was approaching, allowing divorced spouses to claim a share of employment-related pension benefits accumulated during marriage, and some men feared it would finally give financially dependent wives the means to leave.

“All the men I know are scared. We’re all scared,” he told her.

A 2026 Cabinet Office study has since found that the reform led to an increase in divorces, suggesting that the prospect of greater financial security had made it easier for some women to leave their marriages.

What the Numbers Don’t Explain

Japan’s changing divorce figures don’t tell us exactly why individual marriages end, or whether couples are becoming less willing to work through their differences. But as people live even longer and ideas about marriage continue to evolve, the prospect of spending several more decades together is becoming a question that some couples are willing to reconsider, even after 20 years or more.

The year might be drawing to a close, but it's a perfect time to do something new with your Japanese study! Take a look below at the latest list of Japanese learning resources, lovingly selected by our team, to help supercharge your Japanese study.

Activate Your Japanese!

Activate Your Japanese! is a 24-episode drama about a Vietnamese girl named Xuan who came to Japan to work in a hotel. It comes from Japan's national broadcasting network, known as NHK, which is known for producing quality video content about all sorts of topics. You can think of them as the BBC or CNN of Japan. In the drama, she encounters a sentient keychain, new friends, and lots of new Japanese. And as with any drama, there are elements of humor and romance that really make it entertaining.

Each video is divided into parts: The main skit, Today's Strategy, Onomatopoeia, and Welcome to My Japan. The main skit follows Xuan and her time adjusting to Japanese life, all while providing useful communication strategies. Next, the Today's Strategy section focuses on a useful communication strategy or phrase that Xuan utilized in the main skit. Plenty of examples are provided, making this part of each video particularly useful for learners. Then comes the Onomatopoeia bit, which introduces a common Japanese onomatopoeia. Again, several examples are provided to help reinforce how the word is used in real life. And finally, the Welcome to My Japan bit finishes off each video with a presentation of someone's life after coming to Japan. Many of these individuals immigrated to Japan for work and have lived in the country for several years. Their work, interests, and hobbies are highlighted in this section.

Every video in this series comes with translated captions and even a transcript, making it ideal for learners at level who want to practice reading or listening skills. But even if learning Japanese is not your main goal, the series can still be enjoyed purely as a drama for one's own entertainment. According to the site, this series will be available until 2027, so there's plenty of time to go through each of the 15-minute episodes.

Beyond Activate Your Japanese!, the NHK has a number of other resources for Japanese learners, like the Essential Japanese section, which provides survival phrases, and Easy Japanese: Conversation Lessons, which contains lots of learning content related to conversation practice. There's something for everyone, so check it out!

あかね的日本語教室

VIDEO

あかね的日本語教室, otherwise known as Akane's Japanese Class, is a popular YouTube channel produced by a Japanese teacher named Akane. This channel is targeted towards intermediate and advanced learners. However, Akane mentions that this channel is also accessible to beginners who want a bit of a challenge. The difficulty comes from all the videos being entirely in Japanese. The subtitles at the bottom of the screen are in Japanese, and include furigana over more difficult kanji. There are also closed captioning subtitles that can be turned off and on, with an impressive number of languages covered — 15!

The videos on this channel are very educational while also entertaining. The topics surround learning Japanese, travel around Japan, everyday life in Japan, and more. An example of Akane's videos that Japanese learners may find most useful are "[Business Japanese] Basics of telephone correspondence" and several interviews with non-native speakers living in Japan and studying the language. Each video lasts about 10-15 minutes in length, and they go by quickly. Because Akane speaks slowly, it's easy to follow the dialogue. If you're looking for even more content by Akane, you can also check out the podcast and Instagram page she also has.

Japanese Immersion with Asami

Japanese Immersion with Asami is a YouTube channel that, as the name suggests, focuses on teaching via comprehensible input; that is, Japanese made as easy to understand as possible, even for beginners, without relying on English explanations or translations. Asami has been a Japanese teacher since 2015, and with her trusty partner Hyougen, mostly reads stories in her videos, with helpful explanations and commentary; all in Japanese.

The videos are a great way to get your feet wet engaging with Japanese media more, without feeling like you're alone in the endeavor. In fact, the casual, supportive atmosphere of her videos might be their best feature; it really does feel like a private lesson. And with several series in a variety of genres and titles, such as Kiki's Delivery Service and short stories, you're sure to find a narrative that piques your interest.

日本語表現インフォ

One of the most difficult parts of learning another language can be expressions. As language conveys culture, each individual language has different expressions relevant to its own culture, and translating between them is no easy task. Thankfully for Japanese learners, there's the helpful website 日本語表現インフォ, or "Japanese Expression Info" to make things a little easier.

The site is very straightforward, with various expressions grouped into different categories, like expressions conveying emotions, sensations, or people, for example. From there they're often broken down even further, like expressions relevant to conveying different degrees of sadness.

While the website states the intent was to be a resource for people aiming to write in Japanese, it's helpful for Japanese learners as well. Not only will using these sorts of expressions add a sense of naturalness to your own writing, but they might help you while reading Japanese. 日本語表現インフォ is a great resource for learning both Japanese language and culture.

Sail

Sail is a unique approach to Japanese language exchange apps. Available on iOS and Android, Japanese learners first register for an account, filling out some of their interests and a basic self-introduction. But rather than connect with teachers or other language learners, Sail connects you to native Japanese speakers in the form of retirees and senior citizens. Like all similar apps, you're able to look at the profiles of various exchange partners, and find someone who might be a good fit in terms of interests and availability. Conversations are set to last 25 minutes, offering a contained experience: long enough that you're able to actually chat, but not so long that you might run out of steam.

It's a unique concept, and one that works well. Older people make good conversation partners, and are often very cordial and have a lot of free time. They're excited to get the chance to connect to learners, and share something of their language and culture, and this eagerness is contagious. What's even better is that Sail allows for unlimited conversations for a simple fee of $14.90 a month, with discounts at longer terms. This makes Sail one of the best bangs for your buck for Japanese learners hoping to converse.

パパパパパピィ

Update: Sadly this resource is no longer available.

Do you miss the good ol' days of reading picture books as a kid? Would you like to know more about Japanese children's books and the colorful images and themes they have inside? With the YouTube channel パパパパパピィ, you can read along, in a bedtime story fashion, to many different Japanese children's books.

Each story is read front to back by the host of the channel, who keeps you engaged with different voices and sounds, depending on the character or noise. You'll be able to follow along with the script, as the pages are shown while being narrated. Picture books are a great resource for beginner learners, as they don't have as many kanji. The readings are very short, witheach video being under ten minutes long. Whether you're looking to find more resources for your kids, or you're wanting to bring back the nostalgia of reading children's books, give this channel a go and watch how you're instantly transported to the land of cheery Japanese stories!

Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures

If you're wanting to get more listening practice in, the podcast Megumi's Daily Japanese Adventures could be the right fit for you. This podcast was created for Japanese learners and could be used somewhat similarly to JLPT listening practice. In this podcast, the host, Megumi, talks about various experiences she's had related to travel, Japanese culture, and more. The way Megumi describes these adventures is story-like, with background music to accompany her anecdotes and detailed accounts. She speaks slowly and clearly, which is good for those who are just beginning to listen to content that's entirely in Japanese. The targeted audience for this podcast is around the intermediate level.

For listeners who would like to follow along with the dialogue, there are also transcripts on Megumi's website. At the end of these transcripts, there are English translations for some of the more advanced vocabulary. The episodes are around 5 minutes in length, so they're quick listens if you want to give them a go.

Human Japanese

Made by the same people who brought us Satori Reader, the Human Japanese apps are basically digital textbooks for Japanese, or as they call it, your "personal sensei in a box." There is an app for beginners and then an intermediate-level version. The beginner version boasts over 500 pages of content and around 800 example sentences, with breakdowns of each word and particle to boot! When teaching kana and kanji, there are stroke order animations, and plenty of example words as well.

The lessons in this app are truly worded and organized like a textbook. You will find lessons related to food, school, geography, health, work, and the weather. Major grammar points are included as well, including lessons on verbs, adjectives, adverbs, conjugations, counting, particles, and more. At the end of each lesson, you can find review quizzes. By default, you cannot move on to the next chapter until you have passed a chapter review quiz, but you can change this in the settings.

The overall design of the app is sleek and nice, but can feel a little dated to some seeing as it was originally created over a decade ago. Some pages are a little intimidating because of their word count, which some may find annoying. And there are no romaji to help you out; the app assumes you will learn hiragana and katakana. So if this kind of electronic textbook is just what you're looking for, then Human Japanese may be for you. For readers looking to give it a try, they offer a lite version free of charge.

YomuJP

For the Japanese graded reader junkies out there looking for more material, you might want to check out YomuJP. This website is dedicated to providing Japanese learners with easy, level-appropriate reading content in a simple layout.

There are tons of writings in their database. Each article contains pictures, and even audio recordings of a native speaker reading the material. This means you can use this site for listening practice as well. The stories are separated by reading difficulty. There are six categories, from N6 to N1, with N6 being the easiest (introductory level Japanese) and N1 being the hardest (advanced Japanese). According to the site, this scale is based on the Japanese Language Proficiency Test (JLPT) with N6 being an even easier level than the JLPT's lowest level of N5. You can browse articles by difficulty level or by tag.

The site also regularly posts to their Twitter page, often highlighting articles. New articles seem to be consistently released as well. If you are interested in practicing your reading (or listening) skills, or if you are thinking of studying for the JLPT, then consider YomuJP as one handy-dandy tool in your toolbox.

Thanks so much for following along with us to the end of the year, and the end of the article! We hope it's been a helpful journey. From all of us at Tofugu, hope you have a relaxing 正月, and spring is right around the corner.

items.text:
Bill Gurley spent years on Wall Street, built his career as a partner at Benchmark, worked through Uber’s hypergrowth era, and now serves on the board of the Santa Fe Institute, where he studies complexity and systems thinking.

Featured clips

Obsessive Learning in Founders

The Craft of Storytelling and Writing

Available Now: YouTube | Spotify | Apple Podcasts | Transcript | X

In this episode, Bill shares the mental models he returns to most often, including systems thinking, second- and third-order effects, and the importance of understanding both the bedrock of your field and the bleeding edge.

He explains what separates great founders, why storytelling and product instincts matter, how he uses AI across different models, and what he sees coming in open source, China, stablecoins, tokenization, payments, and venture capital.

+ Check out Runnin’ Down a Dream: How to Thrive in a Career You Actually Love

++ Check out the Granola Notes

Tiny Lessons

Trajectory matters more than the starting place.

“Success requires balancing a deep knowledge of history with an obsessive focus on the technological edge where disruption happens.”

“I think more people would benefit by studying the history of whatever field they’re in.”

“If it’s tedious to learn, it isn’t a passion. I don’t think you’re in the right lane.”

“I think that anybody in any field should want to be curious about the bleeding edge and what happens.”

“You should understand the really old stuff, the history, because it’s differentiating and shows a passion and it gives you a great frame of mind, but you also want to really understand the new edge. If you do both of those things, I think you’re a power player in your field.”

“If you have to write it out and make it stand alone and be cogent, you’ll think through more of the problems and it’ll be more cohesive and you’ll figure out the loose ends and you’ll tie them up.”

“If regulation gets extremely difficult and mundane and expensive, that could actually lead to more oligopoly.”

“I would describe complex systems as multivariable nonlinear systems. And multivariable nonlinear systems are very hard to predict. They can behave one way for a long time, and then one variable can switch and they can behave another way—the weather, stock markets, all these things. There are consequences that can be first, second, or third-order. You can’t just think with a linear model or just think about one variable because things can go way off the path. You need to be aware that if you make a change here, it could change something here, which could change something there, and it has to be the whole system.”

“You’ve got to be really conscious of the consequence and not get too deterministic about a single metric or a single variable.”

“I’ve always thought of Wall Street as the buyer of the product that venture capitalists create because the eventual liquidity is either an M&A (merger and acquisition) or an IPO (initial public offering).”

One question to ask before hiring or investing in someone: Is this person going to do this no matter what?
